game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Before any dice are revealed, the public fair value is the expected sum, 10.5. I quote symmetrically around it, with each side set to maximise expected profit against the two counterparty types.

- **Noise traders** (65%): on the ask side, expected profit is P(V > A) × (A − 10.5). On the bid side it is P(V < B) × (10.5 − B), with V ~ N(10.5, 4.4).
- **Informed traders** (35%): they buy only when the sum exceeds my ask, and sell only when it falls below my bid, so they cost me E[(S − A)⁺] and E[(B − S)⁺] respectively.

Checking candidate asks against the 3-dice distribution, expected profit peaks near A ≈ 14.5 (about 0.43 on that side). By symmetry the best bid is B ≈ 6.5, giving a total expected profit of roughly 0.86 for this quote.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 14.5}

Die 1 is 4, so the fair value is 4 + 3.5 + 3.5 = 11. The unrevealed sum has standard deviation about 2.4, and noise traders' valuations have standard deviation 4.4. Choosing a symmetric half-spread to maximise expected profit against the informed/noise mix gives a half-spread of about 3.7. Rounding to ticks (bid down, ask up) gives a bid of 7.2 and an ask of 14.8, the same as quote 3.

{"bid": 7.2, "ask": 14.8}

Known dice total 10 (die 1 = 4, die 2 = 6). Die 3 is uniform on 1 to 6, so the public fair value is 10 + 3.5 = 13.5.

The informed counterparty can only see a settlement between 11 and 16. Quoting outside that range means it never trades against us, so only noise traders can hit our prices. Their valuation is 13.5 + N(0, 4.4), so I'll set each side where the expected profit per noise trade times its trade probability is largest.

- **Ask:** profit is (A − 13.5) × P(noise buys) = (A − 13.5) × (1 − Φ((A − 13.5)/4.4)). This is maximised near A ≈ 16.8, which is above the informed threshold of 16.
- **Bid:** by symmetry, B ≈ 10.2, which is below the informed threshold of 11.

Each side then has about a 23% chance of a noise trade at a 3.3 edge. The fair value doesn't change before quote 6, so the same quotes hold for the final quote.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 16.8}

Public fair value is 4 + 6 + 3.5 = 13.5, and settlement is 10 + die 3, so it lies in {11,…,16}. Informed traders only trade when the settlement is on the wrong side of my quote, so I can't profitably quote inside the range where they would trade. Noise traders' expected profit per side is maximised where P(trade) × distance from fair value peaks, at about 3.3 from 13.5 with noise sd 4.4 (about 0.75 standard deviations).

- **Ask:** at 16.8 the informed buy-side term is zero, since no outcome exceeds 16.8, and the noise-trader term is about 0.486. Nearby asks (16.0, 16.9, 17.0) are slightly lower, and asks below 16 are hurt by informed buyers.
- **Bid:** the mirror image gives 10.2. The informed sell-side term is zero because no outcome falls below 11, and the noise-trader term is about 0.486.

I'm at position 0 on the last quote, so there's no inventory to manage.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 16.8}

Informed traders can hit a quote only when it's mispriced against the true sum, so I set the bid where the marginal adverse-selection loss from informed sellers offsets the expected gain from noise sellers. That comes out near 6.6. The distribution is symmetric about 10.5, so the ask mirrors it at 14.4. My +1 position doesn't change the expected-value calculation.

{"bid": 6.6, "ask": 14.4}

That favours a fairly wide quote, roughly 9 to 15 around 12. I'm slightly lowering the ask to 14.5 to make selling to us more likely, since we're long one unit.

Die 3 is still hidden, so the public fair value is 5 + 4 + 3.5 = 12.5. An informed counterparty knows the settlement value exactly, which is 9 + die 3, so it lies in 10 to 15. Noise traders are uninformed.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer never buys at 15.8 because the value cannot exceed 15. Noise traders buy when their valuation exceeds 15.8 (about 22% of the time given their noise), and each such sale earns 15.8 − 12.5 = 3.3. Around 15.8 this maximises expected profit.
- **Bid:** Symmetrically, an informed seller never sells at 9.2 because the value cannot be below 10. Noise traders sell when their valuation is below 9.2, and each purchase earns 12.5 − 9.2 = 3.3 in expectation.

Both quotes sit outside the informed trader's possible values, so the expected trading profit is positive and adverse selection is zero. The position is +2, so the bid can still be hit once before the +3 limit pulls it.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 15.8}

**Quote 6 reasoning**

- Die 3 is the only unknown, so settlement V = 9 + die 3 is uniform on {10,...,15}, with public fair value 12.5.
- Noise traders are independent of V, so their trades earn a fixed edge against 12.5. Informed traders only trade when V is outside my quote, so they cost me nothing if both quotes sit outside {10,...,15}.
- For the ask, the noise-trader edge is 0.65 · P(X > A) · (A − 12.5), with X ~ N(12.5, 4.4). Setting A ≥ 15 keeps informed buyers out. Maximising over A gives A ≈ 15.8.
- For the bid, the same logic with B ≤ 10 keeps informed sellers out. Maximising 0.65 · P(X < B) · (12.5 − B) gives B ≈ 9.2.
- Position +2 does not change the expected-value calculation, since I value the position at the fair value of 12.5.

Subtracting the informed buyers' expected losses (0.2 · Σ over S > ask of p(S)·(ask − S)), the ask-side edge peaks near 13 (about 0.34 per quote). The 9.5/11.5 quotes from before earn only about 0.14. The distribution is symmetric about 10.5, so the bid mirrors the ask at 8.

A half-spread of about 2.5 gives the best expected edge (about 0.37 per side), and 14.5 / 9.5 is symmetric around 12.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 14.5}

game.title: Dice sum

Profit is roughly flat near a half-spread of 7, with a spread of 1 clearly losing money. I'm quoting bid 5.5 and ask 19.5.

The unconditional fair value is 12.5 (die means 3.75 + 2.5 + 6.25). The earlier sale to me at 5.5 suggests a low sum, since informed sellers only hit bids above the settlement value. Updating on that trade (and iterating the fair value, since noise traders price off the public posterior) gives a posterior mean of about 9.5.

With that posterior, informed traders only trade against me in the tails, while noise traders trade whenever their valuation crosses my quote. Checking expected profit per side:
- Bid: expected profit peaks around 2.0, where noise sellers are rare but profitable, and informed sellers (only when the sum is below 2) are rare.
- Ask: expected profit peaks around 18 to 19, where noise buyers are rare but profitable and informed buyers (only when the sum is above 18) are rare.

I'm already +1 long at cost 5.5, so these quotes also leave room to add or reduce inventory as the game proceeds. This is a one-step model with rough arithmetic, so the exact levels are approximate.

I set the bid near the break-even point for a sell to us (about 2) and the ask where a buy from us stops being profitable (about 15), since a sale is likely informed when the sum is high.

Fair value is 0 + 2.5 + 6.25 = 8.75, since die 1 = 0 is public and dice 2 and 3 have expected values 2.5 and 6.25. Die 3 is not revealed until stage 3, so it is still unknown.

For each side I compared expected profit per quote, where a trade is informed with probability 0.5 and noise with probability 0.5:

- **Ask:** profit peaks around 15, with 15.0 slightly ahead of 15.5 and 16. It is negative at 10, so asking near fair value is costly.
- **Bid:** profit peaks around 2.0 to 2.5, with 2.0 slightly ahead. It falls off above 5.

Both sides are close to flat across their best range, so the choice within each range matters little. I'm keeping the bid at 2.0 and the ask at 15.0, the same as quote 3.

Die 2 has mean 2.5 and die 3 has mean 6.25, so before any trade history the fair value is 0 + 2.5 + 6.25 = 8.75. The trade history shifts this. The sell at 5.5 points to a low sum, and the two buys at 15 point to a high sum, so the posterior is spread out with mass near 0-4 and near 16-18.

Because the informed counterparty trades only when it knows the sum is past my price, I quote where the expected settlement value conditional on a trade still favours me:
- **Ask at 17.0:** a buyer here is most likely informed with a sum of 18, so the conditional expected value is about 14.1. That leaves a positive expected edge per trade, and the ask is near the best point in my rough calculation.
- **Bid at 2.1:** a seller here is most likely informed with a low sum (0-2) or a noise trader, so the conditional expected value is about 4.2. That also leaves a positive expected edge.

These numbers come from a rough Bayesian update, so treat the exact prices as approximate.

- Known so far: die 1 = 0, die 3 = 9. Die 2 is hidden, with mean 2.5. So the public fair value is 0 + 2.5 + 9 = **11.5**.
- The settlement value V is 9, 10, 11, 13 or 18, with probabilities 3/8, 1/8, 1/8, 2/8, 1/8.

**Ask:** An ask of 18.0 leaves no informed buyer, since V ≤ 18. Noise buys with probability about 0.13, earning roughly 6.5 per sale. Lowering the ask adds informed-buyer losses at V = 18 that outweigh the extra noise flow, so 18.0 is about optimal.

**Bid:** A bid of 9 or below leaves no informed seller, since V ≥ 9. Within that range, the noise-only objective (11.5 − B)·P(noise sells) peaks near B ≈ 7.1 after rounding down to the 0.1 grid.

Both sides are expected-value positive on their own, and the position of −1 is well within limits.

- **Ask:** Informed buyers trade whenever V > ask, which is costly below 18. At 18, no informed buyer can trade (V ≤ 18), and the noise-trader edge is still high, so 18 gives the best expected edge.

Both sides together give about +0.49 on the bid and +0.43 on the ask in expected edge. The position of −2 doesn't change the expected-value calculation, since I'm risk-neutral. I've ignored any small upward tilt in fair value from the earlier buys at 15 and 18.

**Quote choice.** Expected profit per quote is maximised where the marginal noise-trader gain balances the marginal adverse-selection loss from informed trades:

**Ask:** The highest possible value is 9, so an ask of 9.0 is never lifted by an informed buyer. A noise buyer arrives with probability about 4.6%, with an edge of about 4.73. Asks below 9 pick up informed buys of the 9-valued card, which costs more than the extra noise flow brings in.

Both quotes are free of adverse selection this round.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Settlement is min(9, 14, card 3) = min(9, card 3). The unrevealed card 3 comes from the 10 remaining cards (one 1, four 3s, two 9s, three 14s), so its distribution is 1: 0.1, 3: 0.4, 9 or 14: 0.5. That makes settlement 1, 3, or 9 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.5, and the public fair value is 5.8.

Informed counterparties trade only when they can profit against my quote, and noise traders are centred on 5.8 with SD 2.8. Expected profit per side:

- **Ask:** At 9, informed buyers never appear, since settlement can't exceed 9. Noise buyers arrive with probability about 0.13, each earning about 3.2 on average, for an expected contribution of roughly +0.20. Lower asks bring in informed buyers at settlement 9, which turns the ask-side expectation negative.
- **Bid:** At 3, only informed sellers at settlement 1 trade, costing about -0.10. Noise sellers arrive with probability about 0.17, each earning about 2.8, for roughly +0.23. The net is about +0.13, which beats a bid of 1 (about +0.10) and any higher bid.

Quote 6 is still to come, so inventory and the updated fair value after a trade will matter, but this quote is best set myopically.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 9.0}

**Settlement value:** Cards 1 and 2 are 9 and 14, so the contract settles at min(9, 14, card 3) = min(9, card 3). The remaining 10 cards are {1, 3, 3, 3, 3, 9, 9, 14, 14, 14}, so card 3 is 1 with probability 0.1, 3 with 0.4, and 9 or 14 with 0.5. That gives settlement 1, 3, or 9 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.5, and a fair value of 5.8.

**This is the last quote,** so only this quote's expected profit matters. Position is 0, and noise traders' trades are independent of settlement, so each side's expected profit is:

- **Bid b:** informed sellers (value below b) cost us, and noise sellers (valuation below b) earn us 5.8 − b on average. The expected profit peaks around b ≈ 2.7–2.9 at about 0.123. Bid 3.0 gives about 0.122, and bid 1.0 gives about 0.10.
- **Ask a:** informed buyers only exist when settlement is above a. Ask 9.0 is best: informed buyers with value 9 do not trade at exactly 9, and noise buyers pay 9 − 5.8 = 3.2 on average, for about 0.20. Asks just below 9 lose to informed buyers, and asks above 9 lose noise-buyer margin.

Bid 2.8 and ask 9.0.

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** The minimum of 3 cards dealt from 12 has distribution P(1)=55/220, P(3)=130/220, P(9)=31/220, P(14)=4/220. So E[min] = 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Adverse selection:** Informed counterparties trade only when their known value is on the wrong side of my quote. Noise traders trade when their valuation (centred on 3.55, sd 2.8) crosses my quote.

- **Ask:** Asks below about 9 let informed buyers take the 9 and 14 outcomes at a loss. At 9.0, only the 14 outcome (prob 4/220) gives informed buyers a profit, and noise buyers rarely reach 9. Net expected profit per quote is about +0.025, which beats 8.9 (+0.021) and 9.1 (+0.021).
- **Bid:** At 1.0, informed sellers never trade, since the minimum value 1 is not strictly below 1. Noise sellers arrive about 18% of the time, for an expected profit of about +0.23 per quote. That beats 0.9 (+0.23), 1.1 (+0.22) and 1.5 (+0.18).

Both sides have small positive expected value under this one-quote analysis, so I quote both.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Without new information, the public fair value is E[min] = 39/11 ≈ 3.55, with P(min=1) = 0.25, P(min=3) ≈ 0.59, P(min=9) ≈ 0.14, and P(min=14) ≈ 0.02.

- **Ask:** Above 9, only a valuation of 14 is worth buying at, and the chance of that is small. At an ask of 9.0, the expected gain from noise buyers outweighs the informed-buyer loss, and moving the ask higher or lower reduces the expected profit.
- **Bid:** A bid near 1 avoids informed sellers, since only a settlement of 1 would sell to us, and it still captures noise sellers who value the contract below the bid. A bid around 1.1 is about optimal for this trade-off.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 9.0}

**Fair value:** Card 1 = 9, so settlement = min(9, card 2, card 3). Cards 2 and 3 come from {1, 3×4, 9×2, 14×4}. The 1 is 10 of 55 pairs, and the seller who took our 1.1 bid last quote was either informed (which requires settlement 1) or a low-valuation noise trader. Updating on that sale gives roughly:
- P(settle = 1) ≈ 0.58
- P(settle = 3) ≈ 0.28
- P(settle = 9) ≈ 0.14

So public fair value ≈ 2.67, and noise valuations centre there.

**Bid:** Any bid of 1.0 or below cannot be hit by an informed seller, since the minimum settlement is 1. Noise sellers arrive when their valuation is below the bid, and expected profit per sale is about 2.67 − bid. That is maximised around 0.5–0.6.

**Ask:** Any ask below about 9 attracts informed buyers when settlement is 3 or 9, which loses money. An ask of 9 cannot be hit by an informed buyer, since settlement is at most 9. It only attracts noise buyers, which is a small but safe positive expectation.

Quote: bid 0.5, ask 9.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 9}

**Key inference:** Quote 2's sale at 1.1 was almost certainly the informed counterparty. A noise trader (valuation about N(8, 2.8) before any reveal) would sell at 1.1 less than 1% of the time, while an informed trader sells at 1.1 only if the settlement is 1. Combined with card 1 = 9, the settlement is 1 with probability about 0.96, 3 with about 0.03, and 9 with about 0.01. The fair value is therefore about 1.16.

**Quote:**
- **Bid 0.0:** Settlement is at least 1, so an informed seller never hits this bid. Noise sellers with valuation below 0 still give a small positive edge.
- **Ask 3.5:** The informed buyer only takes it if the settlement is 9 (about 1%). Noise buyers valuing the contract above 3.5 still buy, and selling the long position there is profitable against the 1.16 fair value.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 3.5}

Settlement is effectively known: the contract settles at the minimum of the three dealt cards, and card 2 = 1 is the lowest value in the deck, so settlement is 1. The public fair value is therefore 1, and position size doesn't add risk.

That means every trade is profitable only if it prices away from 1, and informed traders (who know the value is 1) will only trade against quotes that bracket 1. So I'll keep bid ≤ 1 ≤ ask and earn the edge from noise traders.

- Bid side: expected edge = 0.5 × Φ((b−1)/2.8) × (1−b). Maximising d·Φ(−d/2.8), where d = 1−b, gives d ≈ 2.1 (from Φ(−t) = tφ(t), t ≈ 0.75), so b ≈ −1.1.
- Ask side: symmetric, a ≈ 1 + 2.1 = 3.1.

Both sides give an edge of about 0.48 per quote. The negative bid is unusual, and the rules don't forbid it. If negative prices are not allowed in practice, the fallback is a bid of 0.0, which earns about 0.36 per quote.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

Settlement is already fixed. Card 2 = 1 is the minimum possible value, so the contract settles at 1 regardless of card 3. Public fair value is 1, and informed counterparties know it's 1.

Since nobody has an information edge over me, I only profit from noise traders, and only when I quote away from 1:
- **Bid:** a noise seller hitting my bid at b earns me (1 − b). I maximise (1 − b) × P(noise valuation < b), where valuation ~ N(1, 2.8). That is roughly 2.1 below 1, so b ≈ −1.1. Informed sellers never hit this bid, because they only sell when value < b.
- **Ask:** a noise buyer lifting my ask at a earns me (a − 1). I maximise (a − 1) × P(noise valuation > a), which gives a ≈ 3.1 by symmetry. Informed buyers never lift this ask, because they only buy when 1 > a.

At most one counterparty arrives, so the two sides don't interact. Position +2 leaves room for one more buy (to +3) and sells down to −3, and inventory carries no risk because the settlement value is known.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** The settlement is the max of the three dice. Die 2 is hidden, so the public fair value is E[max], averaged over die 2. The max's distribution is P(4)=0.075, P(6)=0.10, P(7)=0.0875, P(8)=0.2625, P(9)=0.075, P(12)=0.40, which gives E ≈ 9.09.

**Quote:** The 20% informed counterparty trades only when the settlement value is on the wrong side of my price, so I need to set both prices against that adverse selection.

- **Ask:** Informed buyers only appear when V > ask. Since P(V=12)=0.4 and V=12 is the largest outcome, the ask that maximises expected profit is around 12.0. Pricing at 12.0 means an informed buyer never trades at a loss to me.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers appear when V < bid. The mass at 4, 6 and 7 pulls the optimal bid down to about 6.8 (6.9 is essentially tied).

Both quotes are rough optima from a simple one-period model that ignores inventory risk, so the bid and ask are not symmetric around fair value.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 12.0}

The public fair value of the settlement is about 9.09. With nothing revealed, that is the expected maximum of the three dice. I quote a spread centred near that value. Both sides show small positive expected profit against noise traders, with some adverse selection from the informed counterparty.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 10.2}

**Fair value:** Die 3 = 1 is known, so settlement is max(D1, D2, 1). Enumerating the 16 equally likely combinations of D1 and D2 gives E[settlement] = 8.125. Settlement takes the values 4, 6, 7, 8, or 12 with probabilities 1/8, 1/8, 1/8, 3/8, 1/4.

**Ask:** Informed buyers take the ask only when settlement is 12. Noise buyers have valuations centred on 8.125 with sd 2.6. Trading off the adverse selection from informed buyers against the noise-buyer flow, expected profit per unit sold peaks around 10.5–10.6.

**Bid:** Informed sellers hit the bid only when settlement is 4 or 6. Noise sellers have the same distribution as above. Expected profit per unit bought peaks around 6.0.

My inventory of +1 doesn't change the per-quote calculation, since profit is risk-neutral and the position is marked at fair value.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.5}

Die 1 is still hidden, so the public fair value is E[max(D1, D2, 1)] = E[max(D1, D2)] = 8.125. Settlement has a long upper tail (12 with probability 1/4), so informed buyers are most likely to hit a high ask, and the ask needs to sit well above fair value.

Expected edge per side, with 0.2 informed and 0.8 noise, and noise valued at N(8.125, 2.6):
- **Ask:** the edge peaks near 10.5 (about +0.27 per quote). Asks of 10 and 11 are close but slightly lower.
- **Bid:** the edge peaks near 6.0 (about +0.30 per quote). Bids of 5.8 and 6.1 are close but slightly lower.

With no inventory penalty in the objective and expected settlement value a martingale, these one-quote optima are the right quotes.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.5}

**Reasoning (brief):**

- Die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 1 are revealed, so settlement = max(8, die 2). Die 2 is 4, 6, 7 or 12, so settlement is 8 unless die 2 = 12.
- The trade history is informative. Two buys at ask 10.5 are much more likely if settlement is 12, because informed buyers only buy at 10.5 when the value is 12. Updating on those buys puts P(settlement = 12) at about 0.6, so the public fair value is about 10.4.
- Noise valuations are therefore centred near 10.4 (sd 2.6). Informed traders buy at my ask when the value is 12 (probability about 0.12) and sell to me at my bid when the value is 8 (probability about 0.08).
- Expected profit per side, with one counterparty per quote and the two sides' events disjoint:
  - Ask: about 0.35 at 12.4. Just below 12 the informed buyers trade and the expectation drops.
  - Bid: about 0.34 at 8.0. Any bid above 8 invites informed sellers at a loss.
- Position is -1, well inside the limits, so inventory does not change the choice.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 12.4}

Settlement is max(8, 1, die 2), so it is 8 with probability 3/4 (die 2 = 4, 6 or 7) and 12 with probability 1/4 (die 2 = 12). The public fair value is 9.

This is the last quote, so only this trade's expected profit matters. The current position of -2 is already marked at fair value and is not a further cost. The informed trader (20%) buys at my ask only if V > ask and sells at my bid only if V < bid. The noise trader (80%) trades on its valuation around 9 with sd 2.6.

- **Ask:** Expected profit peaks near 11.4. Above 8 the informed buyer only takes the ask when V = 12, which costs about 0.05 per point above 12. The noise-trader term is maximised near 11.4 (about 0.31), and any ask at 12 or above does slightly worse.
- **Bid:** Expected profit peaks near 7.0. Bids above 8 meet informed sellers when V = 8, which is a loss. Below 8 there is no informed flow, and the noise-trader term peaks around 7.0 (about 0.35).

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.4}

info.raw:

**Quote reasoning:** The noise traders are centred on 9.09 with σ = 2.6. The 20% informed traders know V, so they buy from me when V is above my ask and sell to me when V is below my bid. Balancing noise-trader flow against this adverse selection gives:
- **Ask ≈ 11.9.** The informed buyers are concentrated at V = 12, which pushes the optimal ask above the noise-trader mean.
- **Bid ≈ 6.8.** Informed sellers are spread across the lower values, which pulls the optimal bid down. The bid is about 2.25 below the fair value, against about 2.8 above it on the ask.

This is a one-shot optimisation. It ignores how fair value will update after the die 3 reveal and after any trades.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 11.9}

The public fair value is E[max] = 9.09 before any update. The quote-1 no-trade result shifts it slightly, to about 9.06, because the settlement value is more likely to sit inside the old spread. Die 2 is unrevealed, so the 12 outcome (about 31% posterior) drives most of the adverse selection on the ask side.

Expected per-quote profit from a noise trader plus the informed-trader loss, evaluated at each candidate price:
- **Ask:** 11.9 gives about 0.317, the best of the candidates I checked. Asking at 12 removes informed buying but loses noise-buyer flow. 11.8 and 12 are both slightly worse.
- **Bid:** 7.0 gives about 0.330, the best of the candidates I checked. Bidding 7.0 avoids the informed sellers at V=7, and the noise term is still strong.

Position is flat, so no inventory skew is needed.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.9}

**Settlement distribution.** Die 3 = 6 is known, so settlement M = max(D1, D2, 6). Die 1 is still unknown and die 2 is never revealed.
- P(M=6) = 1/4, P(M=7) = 1/8, P(M=8) = 3/8, P(M=12) = 1/4
- Public fair value E[M] = 8.375

**Adverse selection.** The informed trader (prob 0.2) knows M. Noise traders (prob 0.8) value the contract at about N(8.375, 2.6), so each noise trade earns the spread against fair value.

**Ask.** An informed buyer arrives only when M > A. For A between 8 and 12 that means M = 12, a loss of 0.2·(1/4)·(12 − A) in expectation. Maximising the expected profit gives an optimum near A ≈ 10.8. The marginal profit is roughly zero at 10.77.

**Bid.** An informed seller arrives only when M < B. For B just above 6, the only informed sales are at M = 6, and the bid at 6.0 yields no informed loss because a valuation of 6 is not below 6. Marginal profit is roughly flat between 6.0 and 6.1, and 6.0 is optimal on the grid.

I'm quoting myopically since position is 0 and the expected gain from each side is positive.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.8}

Die 3 is known to be 6, so the settlement is max(D1, D2, 6). Enumerating the uniform D1 and D2 gives a public fair value of 8.375. The settlement distribution is 6 (1/4), 7 (1/8), 8 (3/8), 12 (1/4).

Only one counterparty arrives per quote, so the bid and ask contributions add. For each side I maximised 0.8·P(noise trades)·(edge vs 8.375) + 0.2·P(informed trades)·(edge vs the informed valuation):

- **Ask:** the expected profit peaks around 10.7–10.8 (about 0.28). Above 11, the informed buyer (V=12) is a bigger drag than the noise flow is worth.
- **Bid:** the expected profit peaks around 6.0–6.1 (about 0.34). At 6.0 an informed seller (V=6) is not strictly below the bid, so it does not trade.

Both quotes match the spread from quote 3.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.8}

Settlement is max(8, die 2), since die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 6. So it is 12 with probability 1/4 and 8 with probability 3/4, giving a fair value of 9.

Since the trade outcomes are disjoint and profit is linear in cash and position, I can price each side separately:

- **Ask:** the informed buyer only trades when settlement is 12, so asks below 12 lose money to it. Noise buyers at ask a contribute 0.8·(a−9)·P(V>a). The sum peaks around a ≈ 11.4, worth about 0.31.
- **Bid:** the informed seller trades only when settlement is 8, so bids above 8 lose money to it. Noise sellers at bid b contribute 0.8·(9−b)·P(V<b). The sum peaks around b ≈ 7.0, worth about 0.35.

I haven't modelled how this trade updates the fair value for quote 6, so this is a one-step optimum.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.4}

Settlement is max(8, 6, die 2). Die 2 is 4, 6, 7 or 12, so the settlement is 8 in three cases and 12 in one. The public fair value is 9. The informed trader knows the value, so it sells to me when the value is 8 and I bid above 8, and it buys from me when the value is 12 and I ask below 12. Noise traders are centred on 9 with standard deviation 2.6.

Maximising expected profit on each side gives:
- **Bid:** about 7.1, where the expected profit from noise sellers is highest and the informed sellers are excluded (they only trade when the bid is above 8).
- **Ask:** about 11.4, which balances noise buyers against informed buyers who trade when the value is 12.

{"bid": 7.1, "ask": 11.4}

game.description: A custom deck of 8 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 13, 1 card worth 14. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** The minimum of two cards from the 8-card deck {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14} has these probabilities: 2 with 7/28, 9 with 11/28, and 13 with 10/28. So E[settlement] = 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Adverse selection:** Informed traders (20%) buy from me only when the settlement exceeds my ask, and sell to me only when it falls below my bid. Quoting tight around 8.68 gives away about 0.67 per quote to informed flow. Wide quotes avoid most of that loss while still earning the spread from noise traders (80%).

**Ask:** Informed buyers never appear above 13, since the settlement cannot exceed 13. Above that, only noise traders can buy, so the ask should maximise (A − 8.68)·P(noise valuation > A). That gives A ≈ 8.68 + 0.75·6.3 ≈ 13.4.

**Bid:** Informed sellers appear only when the settlement is 2, which has probability 0.25. The first-order condition gives B ≈ 2.86, and bids round down, so I post 2.8.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 13.4}

**Quote 2 reasoning**

- **Prior on settlement:** The min of two dealt cards from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14} has P(2) = 7/28, P(9) = 11/28, P(13) = 10/28. Fair value is about 8.68.
- **Inventory:** We are long 1 at 2.8, so we want to shed the position. That means skewing the ask lower to attract buyers and the bid lower to discourage further sellers to us.
- **Ask:** At an ask near 9.5, informed buyers only appear when the value is 13. Conditional on a buy, the expected value is about 9.4, so 9.5 is roughly break-even against adverse selection.
- **Bid:** At a bid near 7.5, informed sellers only appear when the value is 2. Conditional on a sell, the expected value is about 7.9, so 7.5 keeps a small cushion.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 9.5}

Card 1 is 2, and the contract settles at the smallest dealt card, so settlement is 2 for certain. The public fair value is 2, and an informed counterparty also knows 2.

Because the value is known, holding inventory carries no risk, and informed traders can only trade against a quote that sits on the wrong side of 2. Quoting a bid below 2 and an ask above 2 therefore avoids adverse selection entirely. The only question is how wide to go.

A noise trader sells to my bid when its valuation is below the bid, and buys at my ask when its valuation is above the ask. With valuation ~ N(2, 6.3²) and a half-width d on each side, expected profit per side is about 0.8 × d × Φ(−d/6.3). This is maximised near d ≈ 4.7, since the fill probability falls only slowly as the spread widens. That gives a bid of about −2.7 and an ask of 6.7.

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

info.raw:
Fair value is the expected minimum of two cards dealt from the 8-card deck {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14}. P(min=2) = 7/28, P(min=9) = 11/28, P(min=13) = 10/28, so the fair value is about 8.68.

Informed counterparties (20%) know the true value and trade against me whenever it is favourable to them. The settlement value takes only the values 2, 9 and 13, so I can avoid informed flow with prices that sit just outside the values they would exploit:

- **Ask:** At 13.0, an informed buyer would need a value above 13, which never happens. At 9.0 or 9.1 they would buy whenever the card is 13, which loses money. At 13.0 the ask earns about 0.85 in expected profit from noise traders alone.
- **Bid:** At 2.0, an informed seller would need a value below 2, which never happens. At 9.0 they would sell whenever the card is 2, which loses money. At 2.0 the bid earns about 0.78 in expected profit from noise traders alone.

Quoting near fair value (for example bid 8, ask 9) loses money to informed flow.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 13.0}

Fair value: the two dealt cards give a settlement of 2 with probability 7/28, 9 with 11/28, and 13 with 10/28, so E[V] ≈ 8.68. Nothing new is public since quote 1, and the buy at 13 was from a noise trader, which carries no information about V.

- **Ask:** The informed counterparty buys only when V is strictly above the ask, and V never exceeds 13, so an ask of 13 is never hit by an informed trader. It also maximises expected spread income against noise traders, so I'll keep it at 13.
- **Bid:** A bid near 3 captures noise sellers, and the only informed sellers are when V = 2 (probability 0.25). That gives a slightly higher expected value than bids of 2 or 4 to 8, so I'll post 3.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 13}

**Settlement distribution.** Card 1 is 13, so card 2 is drawn from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 14}. The settlement is min(13, card 2), so S = 2 (1/7), S = 9 (2/7), or S = 13 (4/7). Since only one card is worth 14, S can never exceed 13.

**Trade history.** The buy at 13 gives no information about S, because an informed trader would never buy at 13 when S ≤ 13. The sale at 3 is evidence for S = 2, since an informed seller would sell there. Updating on that sale gives roughly P(S=2) ≈ 0.29, P(S=9) ≈ 0.24, P(S=13) ≈ 0.47, so the public fair value is about 8.9.

**Ask.** An informed buyer only trades if S > ask. Any ask at or above 13 is safe from informed flow. Among those, the noise-trader profit (ask − 8.9)·P(valuation > ask) peaks near 13.6, so I quote 13.6.

**Bid.** An informed seller trades if S < bid, which means S = 2 is the only risk when bidding above 2. Balancing the noise-trader edge against that adverse selection gives an optimum near 2.8.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 13.6}

**Fair value.** Card 1 = 13 leaves card 2 uniform over {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 14}, so the settlement value is 2 (1/7), 9 (2/7), or 13 (4/7 across 13 and 14). Stage-1 trades were made before card 1 was revealed, so I updated on them too. Quote 2 (sold to us at bid 3) is evidence for V = 2, since only an informed seller would sell at 3 in that case. Quote 3 (no trade at bid 2.8) counts against V = 2. Combining these gives roughly P(2) ≈ 0.22, P(9) ≈ 0.26, P(13) ≈ 0.52, so the public fair value is about 9.56.

**Ask.** An informed buyer only hits our ask if V > ask, and V ≤ 13, so an ask above 13 faces no informed buyers. Among noise traders, the expected profit per quote is P(X > A)·(A − 9.56), which peaks near A ≈ 14.3.

**Bid.** An informed seller hits our bid when V < bid, which is the V = 2 case (about 0.22 probability). That pulls the optimal bid down from the symmetric point (about 4.8) to about 4.0, where the expected profit is about 0.75.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 14.3}

Quoting around this, the best trade-off between noise-trader flow and informed-trader losses is roughly:
- **Bid 2.0:** the informed seller only sells when the value is below the bid, and the lowest possible value is 2, so this bid carries no adverse selection.

**Adverse selection:** Informed traders buy from my ask only if S > ask, and sell to my bid only if S < bid. Since S is always in {2, 3, 4}, a bid at or below 2 and an ask at or above 4 can never be hit by an informed trader. Noise trades carry no information about S, so they earn the spread in expectation.

**Ask:** An informed buyer takes the ask when V > a, which costs me. Noise buyers take it when their valuation (2.175 + N(0, 1.8)) exceeds a, which earns me a − 2.175. Trading off these terms, the expected value of the ask side is roughly flat between 4.0 and 4.1 and far worse near fair value (about −0.25 at 2.2). I'll post 4.0, slightly below the previous 4.1, since the earlier no-trade weakly suggests a lower value.

**Bid:** At 0, an informed seller never trades (V ≥ 0 is never below 0), so only noise sellers can hit me, at a positive expected edge of about +0.16. Higher bids add adverse selection from the V = 0 outcome (32.5% probability) and do worse, so I'll bid 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4.0}

The settlement is min(die 1, 5) since die 2 is 5. That gives S = 0 (1/4), 2 (1/4), 3 (1/8), 5 (3/8), so the unconditional mean is 2.75. The earlier no-trade results at asks of about 4 are weak evidence against S = 5, because an informed buyer would have bought at 4. That pulls my estimate of fair value down to roughly 2.0–2.75.

- **Bid 0:** Informed sellers never sell to us here, since no settlement is below 0. Noise sellers with valuations below 0 are rare but profitable, so this is the best bid under either fair-value estimate.
- **Ask 4.5:** Informed buyers take this ask only when S = 5. Noise buyers are the main source of profit. The expected profit is about +0.10 to +0.12 under either fair-value estimate, which is roughly as good as asks of 4 or 5 and more robust than either alone.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4.5}

Settlement is min(die 1, 5). Die 1 gives 0, 2, 3 or 5 with probabilities 1/4, 1/4, 1/8 and 3/8, so the public fair value is 2.75.

This is the last quote, so I only need to maximise this quote's expected edge against the two counterparty types:

Lowering the ask lets informed buyers pick us off when the value is 5, which costs more than the extra noise flow brings in.
- **Bid near 0:** an informed seller only hits it when the value is below the bid, so the bid should stay at or below 0.1. Noise sellers arrive about 6–7% of the time at a margin of roughly 2.6. Expected edge is about +0.11 at a bid of 0 and essentially the same at 0.1 or 0.2, so 0 is marginally best.

- **Quotes:** Against that posterior, informed flow is heavy on both sides, so the spread has to be wide. - V=9: 0.10
- V=10: 0.15
- V=11: 0.15
- V=15: 0.25

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
**Quote 1 reasoning**

- **Fair value:** Each flip is heads with probability 0.5·0.5 + 0.5·1 = 0.75, so the expected settlement is 6 × 0.75 = **4.5**. Noise traders are centred there with standard deviation 2.6.
- **Settlement distribution:** P(S=6) ≈ 0.508 because the all-heads coin contributes 0.5 directly. The fair-coin branch gives Binomial(6, 0.5) for the rest, so the distribution is skewed toward 6.
- **Ask side:** An informed buyer only buys when S > ask. Any ask at or above 6 means informed buyers never trade, since S ≤ 6. Among those asks, the noise-trader edge 0.8·P(V > A)·(A − 4.5) peaks around 6.4–6.5 (≈0.35 expected profit per quote). I'll quote **6.5**.
- **Bid side:** An informed seller sells only when S < bid, and low totals are rare, so the adverse cost is small. The noise-trader edge 0.8·P(V < B)·(4.5 − B) combined with the informed cost peaks around B ≈ 2.3–2.5 (≈0.33). I'll quote **2.4**.

This is a single-quote myopic analysis. It ignores inventory effects and the information revealed before stages 2 and 3.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 6.5}

The coin posterior after two heads is 0.8 always-heads and 0.2 fair. That gives expected settlement E[V] = 2 + 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 5.6, which is the public fair value.

The informed trader only trades against a quote when V is on the far side of it. Since V = 6 with probability about 0.81, a bid near 3.6 or an ask near 7.6 faces almost no adverse selection. At those prices the trades come mainly from noise traders, so each side earns about (quote − 5.6) per expected trade. The noise-trader edge is maximised at about 2 points from fair value on each side, giving roughly +0.35 expected profit per side and only about −0.01 from informed flow.

Bid 3.6 rounds down from the optimum, and ask 7.6 rounds up.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 7.6}

Fair value is 5.6 (posterior on always-heads is 0.8, so expected heads in flips 3-6 is 3.6, plus the 2 known heads). The maximum possible settlement is 6, so an ask above 6 can't be taken profitably by an informed buyer. The ask at 7.6 maximises expected profit from noise traders, and the bid at 3.6 is roughly optimal on the same logic.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 7.6}

**Quote 5 reasoning**

- **Posterior on the coin:** Four heads so far gives P(biased) = (1/2)/(1/2 + (1/2)(1/16)) = 16/17. A biased coin means 6 heads, and a fair coin means 4 + 2 × 0.5 = 5 expected heads, so the public fair value is 4 + 33/17 ≈ 5.94.
- **Informed traders:** Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.956, and 5 or 4 otherwise. A bid of 4.0 can't be hit by an informed seller (it would need V < 4), and an ask of 7.9 can't be lifted by an informed buyer (it would need V > 7.9). So neither side faces adverse selection.
- **Noise traders:** Their trade decisions depend only on the public fair value, so each fill earns the spread against 5.94. Choosing the ask to maximise P(buy) × (ask − 5.94) gives about 7.9. Choosing the bid to maximise P(sell) × (5.94 − bid) gives about 4.0. Both are near the optimum.
- **Position:** I am short 1, so the bid also lets me cover toward flat.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

**Fair value:** Four heads in a row has likelihood 1 under the two-headed coin and (1/2)^4 = 1/16 under the fair coin. The posterior is P(two-headed) = 16/17. Under two-headed, the total is 6. Under fair, the expected total is 4 + 1 = 5. So the public fair value is 101/17 ≈ 5.94.

**Adverse selection:** Informed traders see 6 with probability about 0.94, and values of 4 or 5 are rare. An ask of 7.9 is never bought by an informed trader, and a bid of 4.0 is never sold to us by one. Only noise traders can fill these quotes.

**Pricing:** Noise valuations are centred on 5.94 with sd 2.6. Expected profit per side is roughly P(fill) × distance from fair value. That is maximised near 1.95 away from fair value on each side, which gives an ask of about 7.9 and a bid of about 4.0. Both sides give about +0.44 in expectation.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The settlement is the total number of heads in 6 flips. Under the prior, the coin is fair with probability 1/2 (heads count ~Binomial(6, 0.5)) or always heads with probability 1/2 (heads count = 6). So the settlement distribution is bimodal: P(X=6) ≈ 0.51, and P(X=0..5) ≈ 0.008, 0.047, 0.117, 0.156, 0.117, 0.047. The public fair value is E[X] = 4.5.

Informed traders buy from me when X exceeds my ask and sell to me when X is below my bid. Most of the informed mass sits at X=6, so the ask side faces heavy adverse selection. Since only one counterparty arrives, the two sides contribute independently to expected profit.

- **Ask:** Expected profit f(A) = 0.65·P(V>A)·(A−4.5) + 0.35·Σ_{X>A} P(X)(A−X). The kink at X=6 makes A = 6.0 the optimum (about +0.18 per quote). Quoting 6.0 means an informed trader at X=6 does not buy, since 6 is not above 6.
- **Bid:** The symmetric calculation over X ≤ 2 (the informed sellers) gives an interior optimum near B ≈ 2.73. Bids round down, so B = 2.7 (about +0.11 per quote).

This is a myopic one-quote analysis. It ignores how a trade would change inventory and how the reveals before stages 2 and 3 will shift the fair value.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

Public fair value is 4.5: the coin is fair with probability 1/2 (mean 3 heads) or always heads (6 heads), so E[S] = 6 × 0.75 = 4.5. Nothing new is revealed, so the fair value is unchanged from quote 1.

Against the informed trader (35%) and noise traders (65%, valuation about N(4.5, 1.7)), I estimated expected profit per side:
- **Ask at 6.0:** about +0.18. The informed trader never buys because the settlement value cannot exceed 6, and the noise trader's chance of valuing it above 6 is about 19%.
- **Bid at 2.7:** about +0.10. This is close to the best bid (2.6 to 2.7 are roughly equal), and 2.7 matches the previous quote.

Both sides have positive expected edge, so I quote both.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

The public fair value is 4.5: half the time the coin is double-headed (6 heads), otherwise the expected heads is 3, so E[heads] = 0.5·6 + 0.5·3 = 4.5. The settlement distribution is skewed toward 6, since P(6 heads) ≈ 0.52.

Against this, the ask is most profitable at 6. Informed buyers would only take it if the settlement value exceeded 6, which is impossible, so only noise traders can hit it, at an expected gain of about 1.5 per unit. Asks slightly below 6 bring in informed buyers who pay less than the settlement value.

The bid is roughly flat between 2.5 and 2.8 in expected profit, so I'm keeping it at 2.7 to match the previous quotes.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6}

Two tails are revealed, so the coin cannot be the always-heads coin. The posterior is fair with certainty. The remaining four flips are then Binomial(4, 0.5), so the public fair value is 2.0. Against that baseline, I'm quoting symmetrically around 2.0: a 3.5 ask and a 0.5 bid. A myopic check of expected profit per quote, weighing noise-trader flow against informed adverse selection, puts the best ask near 3.4 to 3.5, and the symmetric bid is 0.5.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 3.5}

The coin is certainly fair: two tails in flips 1 and 2 rule out the always-heads coin. Settlement is 2 known heads plus Bin(2, 0.5), so the public fair value is 3.0 and the settlement distribution is S = 2, 3, 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4.

Because this is the last quote, I only need to price the immediate trade. Adverse selection matters: an informed trader buys at my ask only when S exceeds it, and sells at my bid only when S is below it. For noise traders, the trade is worth (price − 3) on the ask side and (3 − price) on the bid side.

- **Ask:** above 4.0 the informed trader never buys, so only noise traders trade. Expected profit peaks near 4.3 (about 0.188 per quote).
- **Bid:** the mirror image holds. Expected profit peaks near 1.7 (about 0.188).

Both sides are symmetric around 3, and the position of +2 does not change the calculation because profit is linear in position and settlement.

Expected profit per unit at a bid b is 0.65·Φ((b−3)/1.7)·(3−b) plus an informed-trader term of 0.35·Σ P(s)(s−b) over s < b. Evaluating this gives a maximum near b ≈ 1.7–1.8, worth about 0.19 per unit. The ask is symmetric around 3, so the best ask is about 4.3. Rounding bids down and asks up gives 1.7 and 4.3.

Revealed flips 1-4 are H, H, T, T. A T rules out the always-heads coin, so the coin is fair. Flips 5 and 6 are fair coin flips, so the settlement value is V = 2 + Binomial(2, 0.5), taking 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25, and the public fair value is 3.

- **Informed traders** only trade when their valuation (V) is on the wrong side of my quote, which always loses me money. So I want the bid at or below 2 and the ask at or above 4 to avoid them.
- **Noise traders** trade based on fair value 3 plus N(0, 1.7²) noise, so their trades are uninformative about V.
- **Bid:** maximising 0.65 · Φ((b−3)/1.7) · (3−b) gives an optimum near 1.7. Bidding above 2 adds adverse selection, so I stay at 1.7.
- **Ask:** the same logic gives an optimum near 4.3, which is also at or above 4, so no informed buyer can hit it.

Both sides have positive expected value, so I quote both. Any trade at these prices comes from a noise trader, so quote 9 is unchanged. Inventory does not affect expected settlement profit within the ±5 limits.

The coin must be fair: an always-heads coin would have produced heads on flips 3 and 4, but both were tails. So the remaining two flips are fair coin tosses, the settlement is 2 + Binomial(2, 0.5), and the public fair value is 3.0.
