Nothing is revealed yet, so the public fair value is 6 × E[p] = 6 × 0.75 = 4.5. The settlement distribution is a mixture: with probability 0.5 the coin is fair and V ~ Binomial(6, 0.5), and with probability 0.5 the coin always lands heads, so V = 6. That puts P(V=6) ≈ 0.508.

I chose each side to maximise expected profit per quote, with informed traders trading whenever V is past my price and noise traders trading on their normal valuation:

- **Ask:** Around 6.0 the informed buyers drop out (no integer V exceeds 6), and the noise buyers still pay above fair value. Asks just below 6 lose to adverse selection from V = 6 buyers, and asks above 6 lose noise flow. The best is about 6.0, which is consistent with the prior ask.
- **Bid:** Around 2.7 to 2.8 is the best. Bids in that range only face informed sellers with V ≤ 2, and noise sellers still bring fair-value-based profit. Expected profit is about 0.105 at 2.7 and about 0.105 at 2.8, so I'll keep 2.7.

Position +1 doesn't change these calculations, since inventory is valued at the same posterior.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

**Reasoning**

- Flips 1 and 2 are one heads and one tails. Always-heads is ruled out, so the coin is fair with certainty.
- Settlement = 1 + Binomial(4, 0.5), so V ∈ {1,2,3,4,5} with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16. Fair value is E[V] = 3.0.
- Adverse selection: an informed buyer (35%) only buys when V > ask, and an informed seller only sells when V < bid. Noise traders trade at random around 3.0 with sd 1.7.
- Expected profit per unit on the bid side is roughly 0.65·P(noise sells to me)·(3 − b) + 0.35·Σ_{v<b} P(v)(v − b). This peaks near b ≈ 1.6 (about +0.17 per unit), and is essentially flat between 1.5 and 1.7.
- The payoff is symmetric around 3, so the ask-side optimum is the mirror image, a ≈ 4.4.
- My current +2 position is a sunk cost and does not change expected settlement value, so skewing for inventory would only reduce expected profit under risk neutrality. I'll quote symmetrically around the optimum.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

The coin must be fair: an always-heads coin is ruled out by the tails on flip 2. So the remaining four flips are fair, and the public fair value of the total heads count is 1 + 0 + 4 × 0.5 = 3.0.

The informed counterparty knows the exact count S, which is 1 + Bin(4, 0.5), so S ∈ {1,…,5} with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16. Noise traders value the contract at N(3.0, 1.7).

Pricing each side against both trader types, the expected edge is highest near 4.4 on the ask and 1.6 on the bid. At those prices, the noise-trader gain outweighs the adverse selection from the informed trader. The distribution is symmetric about 3, so the two sides mirror each other.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

The revealed flips 2, 3 and 4 are all tails, which is impossible for the always-heads coin, so the coin is fair with certainty. The remaining flips 5 and 6 are each heads with probability 0.5, and the settlement value is 1 + X5 + X6, so the public fair value is 2.0.

Since this is the last quote, only this trade's expected profit matters. Noise traders are centred on 2.0 with standard deviation 1.7, and informed traders adversely select against any quote beyond their settlement value. Maximising the expected gain on each side:

- **Bid:** the noise-trader term 0.65·Φ((b−2)/1.7)·(2−b) peaks near b ≈ 0.73. Informed sellers at S=1 only become a loss above 1.0, so b = 0.7 is best (about 0.188 expected gain). Bidding 0.8 gives about 0.187.
- **Ask:** by symmetry the peak is near a ≈ 3.27. Above 3.0 there is no informed-buyer loss, so a = 3.3 is best (about 0.188 expected gain). Asking 3.2 gives about 0.187.

The position of +2 is already marked at its expected settlement value, so it doesn't change these quotes.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Quote 1 has no revealed information, so the public fair value is E[heads] = 6 × (0.5×0.5 + 0.5×1) = 4.5. The settlement distribution is bimodal: with probability 0.5 the coin is always heads and S = 6, and otherwise S is Binomial(6, 0.5). That makes a wide, asymmetric quote better than a tight one around 4.5.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer takes my ask whenever S > A. Above 6 that never happens, so A = 6.0 gives up no informed adverse selection and still collects noise-trader sales. Expected contribution is about +0.12. Lower asks gain more noise flow but lose more to the 50% chance S = 6.
- **Bid:** An informed seller hits my bid whenever S < B. Around B = 3.0 the noise-trader gain roughly balances the informed loss, with expected contribution about +0.04. Bids of 2.5 and 3.5 are slightly worse.

This is a one-step analysis that ignores how future reveals will change the fair value.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

The prior is a 50/50 mix of a fair coin (expected heads 3) and an always-heads coin (6 heads), so the public fair value is 4.5. The settlement distribution is heavily skewed toward 6 (about 51%), which makes the ask side the main adverse-selection risk.

Expected profit from each side, weighting noise traders at 0.65 and informed traders at 0.35, is separable in bid and ask:
- **Ask:** an ask of 6.0 is never hit by an informed buyer, and noise buyers still take it when their valuation exceeds 6 (about 12%). Lower asks lose more to informed buyers than they gain from noise flow.
- **Bid:** a bid near 3.0 maximises the balance between noise sellers and informed sellers, who sell to us when the value is below the bid.

This is the same quote as quote 1. No trade occurred and nothing new is revealed, so the fair value is unchanged.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

Posterior: two heads so far puts P(fair coin) at 0.2 and P(always-heads) at 0.8. The next flip is heads with probability 0.9, so the public fair value is 2 + 4(0.9) = 5.6. Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.81 (both coins give 6 heads only in the biased case, plus a small fair-coin chance), so informed traders never want to buy above 6.

- **Ask:** Informed buyers can't profit from an ask above 6, so only noise buyers matter. Roughly 6.6 maximises expected profit per quote.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers appear only when settlement is below the bid. Roughly 4.4 balances noise sellers against that adverse selection.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.6}

**Posterior and fair value**

- Two heads in a row gives P(biased coin) = (½·1) / (½·1 + ½·¼) = 0.8, so P(fair) = 0.2.
- The four unrevealed flips (3 to 6) have expected heads of 0.8·4 + 0.2·2 = 3.6, so the fair value is 2 + 3.6 = **5.6**.
- Settlement is almost always 6: P(V=6) ≈ 0.81. The other values are V=5 (0.05), V=4 (0.075), V=3 (0.05) and V=2 (0.0125).

**Ask**

An informed buyer takes any ask below 6, since V = 6 most of the time, and loses us money. Asks at or above 6 avoid that. Among those, the noise-trader term 0.65·(A − 5.6)·P(noise valuation > A) peaks near A = 6.6, worth about 0.144 per quote.

**Bid**

Balancing noise sellers (more likely at lower bids) against informed sellers (who appear when V < B, which costs us), the expected profit peaks at B ≈ 4.3 to 4.4, at about 0.093 per quote. I take 4.4.

No new information has arrived since quote 4, so the optimal quote is unchanged.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.6}

**Reasoning**

- **Posterior on the coin:** Four heads in a row. P(always-heads | data) = 1 / (1 + 1/16) = 16/17 ≈ 0.941, and P(fair | data) = 1/17.
- **Settlement:** Settlement = 4 + (heads in flips 5 and 6). Given always-heads, V = 6. Given fair, V is 4, 5 or 6. So P(V=6) ≈ 0.956, P(V=5) ≈ 0.029, P(V=4) ≈ 0.015.
- **Public fair value:** μ = E[V] ≈ 5.94. Noise traders value the contract at μ ± 1.3.
- **Ask:** Informed traders never buy at an ask above 6, since V ≤ 6. Noise-trader expected profit is about (a − μ)·P(noise valuation > a), which is maximised near z ≈ 0.75, so a ≈ 6.9. At a = 6.9 the expected profit is about 0.144 per quote.
- **Bid:** Noise-trader expected profit is about (μ − b)·P(noise valuation < b), again maximised near μ − b ≈ 0.97. Adverse selection from informed sellers (who only sell when V = 4) is small. Bids of 4.9 and 5.0 both give about 0.139; I pick 4.9.

Quote: bid 4.9, ask 6.9.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

**Quote 8: bid 4.9, ask 6.9**

- **Posterior:** Four heads in a row favours the always-heads coin. P(biased | data) = 16/17, so P(fair) = 1/17.
- **Public fair value:** E[flips 5 and 6] = 16/17·2 + 1/17·1 = 33/17 ≈ 1.94, so F ≈ 5.94.
- **Settlement distribution:** V = 6 with probability about 0.956, V = 5 with about 0.03, and V = 4 with about 0.015.
- **Ask side:** Informed buyers only buy when V > ask, so an ask at or above 6 meets only noise traders. Maximising 0.65·(a − F)·P(noise valuation > a) gives an optimum near 6.9.
- **Bid side:** The same logic gives an optimum near 4.95. Informed sellers only trade when V < bid, which at 4.9 means V = 4, a small adverse-selection cost. The expected profit is about the same at 4.9 and 5.0, so I take 4.9.

Position is 0, so neither side is near the ±4 limits.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Posterior mean after the last trade is about 3.3. The sell at my bid of 3 suggests the true value may be low, and I'm already long one unit. I'll quote a spread around 3.3, with the ask slightly lower to encourage selling back.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 3.9}

My estimate of fair value is about 1.9. The prior mean is 4.5 (a 50/50 mix of a fair coin with mean 3 and a two-headed coin with value 6), but the two sales to us at 3 and 2.6 are strong evidence of low value. Informed sellers only sell when the value is below our bid, so the posterior puts most of its weight on 1 or 2 heads.

Using that posterior:
- **Bid at 1.0:** Informed sellers here are rare (only V=0 is likely, about 4%). Noise sellers, who sell when their valuation is below 1.0 (about 25% chance per noise trader), give a small positive expected profit.
- **Ask at 3.0:** Informed buyers appear only if V≥3, which is about 8.5% under the posterior. Noise buyers, whose valuation is above 3.0 about 20% of the time, give a small positive expected profit. Asks near 2.0 lose money to adverse selection.

Both sides are positive in expectation under this model. The estimate is rough, and the result is sensitive to the fair value assumption.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 3.0}

**Quote 4 reasoning**

- After flips 1 and 2 both came up heads, the posterior is P(double-heads coin) = 0.8 and P(fair coin) = 0.2.
- Settlement is 2 + the remaining 4 flips. Public fair value is 0.8·6 + 0.2·4 = **5.6**.
- Given the posterior, settlement is 6 with probability about 0.81, and otherwise 2 to 5.
- Informed traders (35%) buy only if V > ask and sell only if V < bid. Noise traders (65%) trade around 5.6 with SD 1.3.
- An ask at 6.6 is above the maximum possible settlement of 6, so informed traders never buy there. It also maximizes the expected profit from noise buyers.
- A bid around 4.4 maximizes expected profit from noise sellers while limiting the losses to informed sellers.
- Position is +1, well inside the ±4 limits, and risk-neutral expected profit is the objective, so no inventory skew is needed.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.6}

Posterior after flips 1 and 2 (both heads): P(always-heads) = 0.8, P(fair) = 0.2. Expected settlement is 2 + 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 5.6. The informed buyer only trades on the ask when S = 6, so the ask at 6.6 attracts only noise traders and has positive expected edge. On the bid, the best expected edge is near 4.4, which is also consistent with quote 4.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.6}

**Posterior:** Flips 1 and 2 were both heads. The fair coin gives that with probability 0.25 and the always-heads coin with probability 1. So P(fair | data) = 0.2 and P(always-heads | data) = 0.8. The expected number of heads in the remaining four flips is 0.2×2 + 0.8×4 = 3.6, so the public fair value is 2 + 3.6 = **5.6**.

**Ask side:** Settlement is at most 6, so an informed buyer only trades when the ask is below 6. Setting the ask at 6.6 shuts out informed buyers and still captures noise buyers, whose valuation exceeds 6.6 with probability about 0.22. The expected edge is about 0.14 per quote, which is roughly the best available.

**Bid side:** Informed sellers trade whenever settlement is below the bid, which costs money. Comparing candidate bids, the expected edge peaks around 4.3 to 4.4, at about 0.09 per quote. I'm taking 4.4 since it is the same level as the earlier quotes.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.6}

**Fair value.** Four heads in four flips gives posterior P(two-headed coin) = 16/17. Flips 5 and 6 then have expected heads 16.5/17 × 2 ≈ 1.94, so the public fair value of the settlement is 4 + 1.94 ≈ **5.94**.

**Settlement distribution.** V = 6 with probability about 0.956, V = 5 with about 0.029, and V = 4 with about 0.015.

**Ask.** Informed buyers only buy if V > ask, and V ≤ 6, so any ask above 6 is safe from informed buyers. Among noise buyers (valuation ~ N(5.94, 1.3)), the expected profit per unit sold, (1 − Φ((A − 5.94)/1.3)) × (A − 5.94), peaks near A ≈ 6.9. Since I'm already long, selling at a premium also reduces inventory. Ask = 6.9.

**Bid.** Informed sellers only sell to me when V < bid, which costs me only when V is 4 or 5. Balancing that against the expected gain from noise sellers, the net expected profit peaks just below 5.0. Bid rounds down to 4.9.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

**Fair value:** After four heads, P(biased coin) = (1/2·1)/(1/2·1 + 1/2·1/16) = 16/17. The settlement is 4 + X5 + X6, so E[settlement] = 4 + 2·(16.5/17) ≈ 5.94. Almost all the probability sits at 6 (65/68), with small weights on 5 (2/68) and 4 (1/68).

**Adverse selection:** Informed traders can only hit my ask if V > ask, and only hit my bid if V < bid. Since V ≤ 6, an ask at 6.9 can't be hit by an informed buyer. Likewise, a bid near 4.9 is only hit by informed sellers when V = 4, which is a small risk.

**Noise-trader profit:** Noise traders are centred on 5.94 with σ = 1.3. Their expected profit per trade is roughly (price − 5.94) on the ask side and (5.94 − price) on the bid side, weighted by the probability they trade. Maximising these gives a distance of about 0.75σ ≈ 0.98 from fair on each side. That puts the ask near 6.9 and the bid near 4.9. Checking nearby prices, the bid at 4.9 is essentially tied with 5.0, and the informed-seller cost at 4.9 is small.

Position limits aren't binding (+1 now), and profit is linear in position, so I'm quoting each side on its own expected value.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

**Posterior:** Four heads in a row. Under the always-heads coin the likelihood is 1, and under the fair coin it is 1/16. So P(always heads | data) = 16/17 and P(fair | data) = 1/17.

**Settlement:** Four heads are already revealed, so settlement is 4 + (heads in flips 5 and 6).
- Always-heads: settlement is 6.
- Fair: settlement is 4, 5 or 6 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4.

This gives P(V=4) = 1/68, P(V=5) = 2/68, P(V=6) = 65/68, and public fair value μ ≈ 5.94.

**Quote:** This is the last quote, so only this trade's expected profit matters. Each side's expected profit is the noise-trader term plus an adverse-selection term from the informed trader.

- **Bid:** Expected profit is maximised near 4.9–5.0, at about 0.139. I pick 4.9.
- **Ask:** Expected profit is maximised near 6.9, at about 0.144. Informed traders never buy at 6.9, since V ≤ 6.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
**Quote 1 reasoning**

With no revealed information, the public fair value is E[heads] = 6 × (½·½ + ½·1) = 4.5. The settlement distribution is a mixture: S = 6 with probability 65/128 ≈ 0.51, and otherwise Binomial(6, ½).

Expected profit per quote is the sum of the two sides, since only one counterparty arrives:
- **Ask:** noise buyers (valuation ~ N(4.5, 1.7)) pay me a − 4.5 on average. Informed buyers only trade when S > a, which costs me. At a = 6.0, informed buyers never trade, since S = 6 is not strictly above 6. The noise contribution is 0.65 × P(V > 6) × 1.5 ≈ 0.18, and the ask side is the best of the candidates I checked (5.8 to 6.1).
- **Bid:** the mass at low values makes informed sellers costly. Expected profit is roughly flat for bids between 2.5 and 2.9, with a peak near 2.7 to 2.8 (about 0.1 per quote).

So the quote is wide and asymmetric, reflecting the bimodal settlement distribution.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

**Quote 2 reasoning (brief):**

- **Prior:** The coin is fair or always-heads with equal probability, so settlement S has mean 4.5. S = 6 with probability about 0.51.
- **Ask at 6.0:** An informed buyer only buys when S > ask, and S ≤ 6, so an ask of 6.0 is immune to informed flow. Noise buyers at 6.0 earn a 1.5 edge over the fair value. This is the best ask in my rough expected-profit calculation.
- **Quote 1 history:** No trade at 2.7/6 is weakly informative. It makes low settlement values (0–2) somewhat less likely, which lifts the posterior mean to about 4.74.
- **Bid at 3.0:** Under the updated posterior, the expected profit from buying at 3.0 is highest among the grid I checked, with 2.9 and 3.1 slightly lower. Informed sellers only sell when S < bid, which limits adverse selection at this level.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

Flip 1 was tails, so the coin cannot be the two-headed one. It must be fair, and flips 3 to 6 are independent 50/50 flips. The fair value of settlement is 1 (flip 2) + 4 × 0.5 = **3.0**.

The settlement distribution is 1 + Binomial(4, 0.5), symmetric around 3. Informed traders buy when settlement is above my ask and sell when it is below my bid, so they pick off stale quotes. Noise traders trade at expected value and give me the spread.

For an ask A, expected profit is 0.65 × P(noise buys) × (A − 3) minus 0.35 × E[(S − A)⁺]. Evaluating:
- A = 3.5: about +0.048
- A = 4.0: about +0.159
- A = 4.4: about +0.173
- A = 4.5: about +0.173
- A = 5.0: about +0.156

The optimum is around 4.4 to 4.5. The distribution is symmetric about 3, so the bid side mirrors it: bid = 6 − ask, giving 1.6. I'll use ask 4.4 and bid 1.6.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

The coin is now known to be fair: flip 1 was tails, which rules out the always-heads coin. The remaining flips are independent fair coins, so settlement is 1 + Binomial(4, 0.5) given the revealed flips. The buy at 4.4 on quote 3 is public information and shifts the fair value up from 3 to roughly 3.5.

With a fair value near 3.5 and a 35% chance of an informed counterparty:

- **Ask 5.0:** An informed buyer only buys when the settlement value exceeds the ask, and the maximum possible value is 5, so an informed trader never buys here. The ask is therefore only exposed to noise traders, and it has the highest expected edge of the ask options I checked.
- **Bid 2.0:** This is roughly the best bid by the same expected-edge calculation. The only informed sale at this bid would come from a settlement of 1, which is unlikely.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 5.0}

**Beliefs about the coin and settlement**

- Flip 1 was tails, so the always-heads coin is ruled out. The coin is fair.
- Flips 5 and 6 are fair and independent. Revealed heads so far is 1 (flip 2), so settlement S = 1 + X5 + X6 ∈ {1, 2, 3}.
- The prior is P(S=1)=0.25, P(S=2)=0.5, P(S=3)=0.25.
- The quote-4 trade (they sold to us at bid 2) is mildly informative. An informed seller sells only if S < 2, i.e. S = 1. Updating on that trade gives roughly P(S=1)=0.41, P(S=2)=0.39, P(S=3)=0.20. Public fair value is about 1.79.
- The quote-3 trade at 4.4 is uninformative now, because it could only have been a noise buyer once flips 3 and 4 came up tails.

**Choosing the quote**

- Informed traders trade only when S is outside my quotes: they buy if S > ask and sell if S < bid. Since S ∈ {1, 2, 3}, an ask of 3.0 or above and a bid of 1.0 or below give no adverse selection.
- Noise traders trade with probability that falls off as my quote moves away from fair value. Expected profit per side is roughly 0.65 × P(noise trader crosses) × distance from 1.79.
- On the ask side, a = 3.1 gives about 0.188 expected profit; quotes inside 3.0 pick up informed buys and lose money.
- On the bid side, b = 0.5 gives about 0.188; the optimum is flat across roughly 0.4 to 0.6.

So I'll quote a wide two-sided market: bid 0.5, ask 3.1.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 3.1}

**Posterior:** Flip 1 = 0 rules out the always-heads coin, since it never shows tails. The coin is fair, so the public fair value is 1 (flip 2) + 0.5 + 0.5 = **2.0**. The settlement S = 1 + H5 + H6 takes values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4.

**Expected profit per side** (noise traders ~ N(2.0, 1.7), informed traders know S; the two sides are mutually exclusive because bid < ask):

- **Ask A:** 0.65 · P(v > A) · (A − 2) + 0.35 · E[(A − S)·1{S > A}]. For A ≥ 3 the informed term is zero, so the noise term dominates. Maximising gives A ≈ 3.3, worth about 0.188.
- **Bid B:** by symmetry around 2, the optimum is B ≈ 0.7, worth about 0.188.

Both quotes are on the 0.1 grid, and the bid is below the ask.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** Expected coin bias is 0.4(0.3) + 0.1(0.4) + 0.5(0.9) = 0.61, so E[heads] = 8 × 0.61 = 4.88 and the public fair value is 10 × 4.88 = 48.8.

**Settlement distribution:** Settlement is 10H, where H is the number of heads in 8 flips. Mixing over the three coins gives a skewed distribution: P(V=0) ≈ 0.025, P(10) ≈ 0.088, P(20) ≈ 0.140, P(30) ≈ 0.130, P(40) ≈ 0.080, P(50) ≈ 0.048, P(60) ≈ 0.083, P(70) ≈ 0.193, P(80) ≈ 0.215. Its standard deviation is about 26, the same as the noise traders' valuation noise, so adverse selection from informed traders is severe.

**Quote choice:** The informed trader (probability 0.35) trades whenever its known value is outside my quotes, so I should price the ask at the point where the informed trader stops buying. I compared expected profit for each candidate:

- **Ask:** Above 80 the informed trader never buys, since V = 80 is the top outcome. At 80, the informed side costs nothing, and the noise-trader edge (about 0.115 probability of a buy, earning 31.2 per trade) gives an expected profit of about 2.3. Asks at 75 to 79 do slightly worse, and asks at 70 or 71 are worse still.
- **Bid:** The best bid is 20. It collects about 2.0 from noise sellers, and the informed loss is about 0.5 from the V = 0 and V = 10 outcomes. Bids at 19 or 21 are nearly as good, and bids of 18 or below are worse.

This is a one-period analysis. Later quotes will benefit from the revealed flips, and trade history may change the fair value. For this first quote, the quotes are bid 20 and ask 80.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 80}

I'm treating the fair value as roughly 42.5, not the unconditional 48.8. The prior mean of heads is 8 × 0.61 = 4.88, which gives 48.8. But the trade at bid 20 is public, and a seller at 20 is more likely when the coin is biased low, so the fair value has moved down. The settlement value has a standard deviation of about 25, and the 35% informed share makes wide quotes worthwhile. Balancing noise-trader flow against adverse selection puts each side roughly 25 from fair value. I'm skewing the ask slightly lower because I'm already long one unit.

{"bid": 17, "ask": 67}

**Fair value:** Flips 1–4 show 3 heads in 4. The posterior over the coin is about 0.16 (p=0.3), 0.08 (p=0.4), 0.76 (p=0.9), so E[p] ≈ 0.765. The four unseen flips give about 3.06 expected heads, so the public fair value is 10 × (3 + 3.06) ≈ 60.6.

**Settlement distribution:** Total heads are 3 to 7, so settlement is 30, 40, 50, 60 or 70 with probabilities of roughly 0.05, 0.10, 0.11, 0.25 and 0.50. The upward skew matters because informed sellers hit a bid when V is below it, and informed buyers lift an ask only when V is above it.

**Bid:** Expected profit per quote from a bid b is the noise-trader term (60.6 − b)·P(noise sells) plus the informed term 0.35·Σ P(V)(V − b) over V < b. This is about 2.7 at b = 40 and drops off quickly above 45 because the informed sellers take the 30 and 40 outcomes. Bid 40 is near the maximum.

**Ask:** Informed buyers can only lift an ask at or below 70 if V = 70 exceeds it, so asks from 70 upward face only noise traders. Expected profit peaks near 80 at about 2.9, and asks at or below 60 are negative.

Quote bid 40, ask 80.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 80}

**Estimate of fair value.** Flips 1 to 4 show 3 heads and 1 tail. Updating the coin prior on that gives P(0.3) ≈ 0.16, P(0.4) ≈ 0.08, P(0.9) ≈ 0.76. The four unseen flips then have an expected 3.1 heads, so settlement is about 10 × (3 + 3.1) ≈ 61.

**Quote 3 no-trade.** A no-trade at bid 40 rules out an informed seller with V < 40, which means V = 30 (all remaining flips tails) becomes less likely. That lifts the fair value to roughly 61.3.

**Ask.** The informed buyer only buys if V > ask, and the highest possible value is 70. For an ask at or above 70, the only expected edge comes from noise buyers, which is 0.65 · P(X > A) · (A − 61.3). With noise sd 26, this is maximised near A ≈ 61.3 + 0.75 × 26 ≈ 81, and at 81 the edge is about 2.87 per quote.

**Bid.** Sales to us come from noise sellers (edge 0.65 · P(X < B) · (61.3 − B)) and from informed sellers when V < B, which costs us. Balancing these gives B = 40, with an edge of about 2.77. Bid 41 is slightly worse, and 39 is worse too.

Position +2 does not change the expected value at settlement, so I am not skewing for inventory. Both prices are already whole numbers, so rounding does not apply.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 81}

**Posterior after flips 1-6 (five heads, one tail):** The coin is 0.3 with probability 0.022, 0.4 with probability 0.020, and 0.9 with probability 0.958. Flips 7 and 8 therefore have expected heads 1.75, and the fair value of the settlement is 10 × (5 + 1.75) ≈ 67.5.

**Possible settlement values:** Since flips 7 and 8 are whole numbers, the settlement is 50, 60 or 70, with probabilities about 0.03, 0.19 and 0.78.

**Adverse selection:** An informed counterparty only trades against a quote that is worse than the true value. An ask above 70 cannot be hit by an informed buyer, and a bid below 50 cannot be hit by an informed seller. Quoting outside that range means only noise traders trade with us.

**Noise-only spread:** Noise traders' valuations are N(67.5, 26), so the spread that maximises expected profit per quote is about 19.5 either side of fair value:
- Ask: maximise (A − 67.5) × P(noise valuation > A), which peaks near A = 87.
- Bid: maximise (67.5 − B) × P(noise valuation < B), which peaks near B = 48.

Both are close to flat near their peaks, and neither side reaches the informed range, so these quotes avoid adverse selection while capturing the widest profitable spread.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 87}

The settlement can only be 50, 60 or 70 (5 heads so far, plus 0 to 2 heads in flips 7 and 8). The posterior puts the expected settlement near 67.5, so that is the public fair value that noise traders are centred on.

- **Ask:** A trade at ask A adds (A − 67.5) in expectation from noise traders. Informed buyers only buy when settlement exceeds A, and that cannot happen for A ≥ 70. The best ask is therefore where the noise term peaks, around 87.
- **Bid:** A trade at bid B adds (67.5 − B) from noise sellers, with probability Φ((B − 67.5)/26). That peaks near 48. Informed sellers only sell when settlement is below B, and that cannot happen for B ≤ 50, so there is no adverse-selection cost at 48.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 87}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The public fair value is 48.8: the expected heads is 8 × 0.61 = 4.88, and settlement is 10 × heads. Because settlement takes only multiples of 10 between 0 and 80, the price levels matter. The distribution of heads is skewed upward (P(8 heads) ≈ 0.215, P(7) ≈ 0.193, P(0) ≈ 0.025), so I compared bid and ask levels directly against that distribution.

- **Ask:** At 80, informed buyers never buy, since their valuation must be strictly above the ask. Noise buyers still trade with about 12% probability, giving an expected edge of roughly 2.3 per quote. Asks of 79 and 80 are essentially tied, and lower asks do worse.
- **Bid:** At 20, informed sellers never sell, since their valuation must be strictly below the bid. The expected edge is about 2.0 per quote, and 19 and 21 are slightly worse.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 80}

**Posterior and fair value.** Flips 1–4 show H,T,T,T, so the likelihood of each coin is p(1−p)³. Weighting by the priors gives posterior weights of about 0.82 on p=0.3, 0.17 on p=0.4, and 0.01 on p=0.9. The expected heads rate is about 0.32, so the expected number of heads in flips 5–8 is about 1.29. Total expected heads are about 2.29, so the public fair value is about 22.9.

**Settlement distribution.** The settlement is 10 × total heads, so it takes values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with probabilities of roughly 0.22, 0.40, 0.28, 0.09, 0.02.

**Quote choice.** Noise traders have valuations around N(22.9, 26), so they are uninformative about settlement. Informed traders trade only when settlement is on the wrong side of my quote, which costs me. I maximised expected per-quote profit:
- **Ask:** the noise-trader term dominates, and the informed-buyer loss only matters at 50. Expected profit peaks near 43 (about 2.83).
- **Bid:** no informed sellers are possible below 10, so the bid is set by the noise term alone. Expected profit peaks near 3–4 (about 2.87). I'll use 3.

Both quotes are far from the previous 20/80, which is too wide to be competitive with the fair value of about 23. Position is 0, so neither side is pulled.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 43}

Posterior on the coin after six flips (2 heads, 4 tails): A (p=0.3) ≈ 0.80, B (p=0.4) ≈ 0.19, C (p=0.9) ≈ 0.004. The expected heads in flips 7 and 8 is about 0.64, so the fair value is about 10 × (2 + 0.64) ≈ 26.4.

The settlement value takes only three values: 20 (≈0.46), 30 (≈0.43) or 40 (≈0.11).

- **Ask:** An informed buyer only buys if V > ask, so an ask of 40 or higher is never hit by an informed trader. Against noise traders (valuation ~ N(26.4, 26)), the expected profit from an ask A is about 0.65 × P(X > A) × (A − 26.4), which peaks near A = 46 (≈2.87). Lower asks pick up informed buys at a loss.
- **Bid:** An informed seller only sells if V < bid, so a bid of 20 or lower is never hit by an informed trader. The noise-trader optimum is near B = 7 (≈2.87).

Both quotes lie outside the support of V, so any trade reveals nothing about the settlement value. The position limits don't bind, and the sides are independent because only one counterparty arrives.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 46}

**Posterior on the coin.** Flips 1 to 6 show 2 heads and 4 tails. The posterior weights are proportional to prior × likelihood: coin A (p=0.3) 0.0086, coin B (p=0.4) 0.0021, coin C (p=0.9) 0.00004. Normalised, that is A ≈ 0.803, B ≈ 0.193, C ≈ 0.004.

**Settlement distribution.** Flips 7 and 8 are unrevealed, so settlement is V = 10 × (2 + heads in flips 7–8). That gives V = 20, 30, 40 with probabilities ≈ 0.463, 0.431, 0.106. The public fair value is μ ≈ 26.43, with noise traders centred there (sd 26).

**Choosing the quote.** This is the last quote, so only this quote's trades matter. My position is −1, so a sale at the bid closes the short and a purchase at the ask extends it.

- **Ask:** Informed traders buy only if V > ask. An ask of 46 is above the maximum possible V of 40, so informed traders never buy. Noise traders buy with probability ≈ 0.226 at a gain of 46 − 26.43, giving an expected contribution of ≈ 0.65 × 4.42 ≈ 2.87. Pushing the ask higher or lower only reduces this, and 46 is the best integer.
- **Bid:** Informed traders sell only if V < bid. A bid of 7 is below the minimum V of 20, so they never sell. Noise traders sell with probability ≈ 0.227 at a gain of 26.43 − 7, giving ≈ 0.65 × 4.42 ≈ 2.87. A bid of 6 is about equal, and 7 is marginally better.

Both quotes avoid informed traders entirely, so the expected gain from this quote is about 5.7.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 46}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Expected settlement with no information: P(heads) = 0.6·0.5 + 0.4·0.8 = 0.62, so E[heads in 8 flips] = 4.96 and the fair value is 5 × 4.96 = 24.8.

With no revealed flips, the main risk is an informed counterparty trading against a stale price. Settlement has a standard deviation of roughly 8.8, so the informed-trader loss is large. Balancing the noise-trader spread premium against that loss gives an optimal half-spread of about 6 on each side. The mixture's upper and lower tails are close to symmetric around 24.8, so the quotes can stay symmetric.

Bid 18.8 and ask 30.8 are both on the 0.1 grid, and the bid is at most the ask.

{"bid": 18.8, "ask": 30.8}

No information has been revealed since quote 1, so the public fair value is still 0.6×0.5 + 0.4×0.8 = 0.62 heads per flip, or 8 × 0.62 × 5 = 24.8. I'll keep the quotes from quote 1, which are symmetric around that value (18.8 and 30.8). A rough check of expected profit per quote, with noise traders at sd 6.6 and informed traders at 20% share, suggests a half-spread near 6 is close to optimal among the options I checked.

{"bid": 18.8, "ask": 30.8}

The public fair value is 8 × 0.62 × 5 = 24.8, and with no flips revealed the settlement has a standard deviation of about 17.5. I checked the expected profit per side against a noise trader (valuation N(24.8, 6.6)) and an informed trader (who knows the settlement). The ask near 30.8 and the bid near 18.8 each come out at roughly +0.6 expected profit. Moving the ask to 26 turns that side negative because of adverse selection, and moving it to 32 lowers it. The bid behaves the same way. Nothing new has been revealed, so I'll keep the same quotes.

{"bid": 18.8, "ask": 30.8}

**Quote 4 (stage 2):** The posterior on the coin is about 70% fair and 30% biased after flips 1 and 2 (0 then 1). The expected settlement is about 5 × (1 + 6 × 0.59) ≈ 22.7, down from the 24.8 prior. The informed trader (20%) buys whenever settlement exceeds my ask and sells whenever it is below my bid. Balancing noise-trader fills against that adverse selection, the expected profit per side peaks near a bid of about 16.6 and an ask of about 29.0.

{"bid": 16.6, "ask": 29.0}

Posterior after flips 1 and 2 (flip 1 = tails, flip 2 = heads) is about 70% fair coin and 30% 0.8-biased coin. The expected settlement is about 22.7, and the settlement spread is wide (sd about 7). Ignoring the inventory effect, which doesn't change expected profit for a risk-neutral objective, the best one-step edge comes from a bid near 17 and an ask near 29. Informed traders are about 20% of arrivals, so these quotes sit well outside the fair value.

{"bid": 17.0, "ask": 29.0}

**Fair value:** Flips 1 and 2 are 0 and 1, so the coin posterior is about 70% fair and 30% biased. The expected heads in the 6 hidden flips is about 3.5, so the public value is about 22.7 before trade history.

**Trade history:** Counterparties bought from us at 30.8 and 29, and no one sold to us at our bids. Buyers at those asks are more likely informed or high-valuing, so I've moved the fair value up to about 25.

**Quote:** Balancing noise-trader flow against adverse selection from the 20% informed traders gives an optimal ask near 30.5 to 31 and an optimal bid near 19 at that fair value. I'm quoting 19.0 and 30.5. The short position of -2 doesn't change expected profit, so I'm not skewing for inventory.

{"bid": 19.0, "ask": 30.5}

**Fair value:** Flips 1–7 show 4 heads and 3 tails. The posterior on the fair coin is P(p=0.5) ≈ 0.78 and P(p=0.8) ≈ 0.22, so P(flip 8 heads) ≈ 0.566. The public fair value is 5 × (4 + 0.566) ≈ 22.8.

**Informed trader:** Its valuation is either 20 (flip 8 tails) or 25 (flip 8 heads). A bid at or below 20 can't be hit by it, and an ask at or above 25 can't lift it.

**Noise traders:** Their valuations are centred on 22.8 with standard deviation 6.6. Maximising 0.8 × P(trade) × edge on each side gives a distance of about 4.96 from fair value on each side. That puts the bid near 17.9 and the ask near 27.8. Both sit outside the informed trader's trading range, so the informed trader adds no adverse selection.

Bids round down, so the bid is 17.8. Asks round up, so the ask is 27.8.

{"bid": 17.8, "ask": 27.8}

**Fair value:** Flips 1 to 7 show 4 heads and 3 tails. The posterior on the fair coin is 0.6·0.5⁷ : 0.4·0.8⁴·0.2³ ≈ 0.781 : 0.219. So P(flip 8 = heads) ≈ 0.781·0.5 + 0.219·0.8 ≈ 0.566.

Settlement is 5 × (4 + flip 8), so it is either 20 or 25, and the expected value is about 22.83.

**Quoting:** Informed traders buy from our ask when the value is 25 and sell to our bid when it is 20. Noise traders have valuation N(22.83, 6.6).

- **Ask:** Pricing above 25 avoids informed buying entirely. Maximising the noise-trader edge (0.8·(a − 22.83)·P(valuation > a)) gives an optimum near 27.8.
- **Bid:** Pricing below 20 avoids informed selling. Maximising the noise-trader edge (0.8·(22.83 − b)·P(valuation < b)) gives an optimum near 17.8.

The position of −2 doesn't change the risk-neutral edge, so the quote stays at 17.8 / 27.8, which is valid (bid below ask).

{"bid": 17.8, "ask": 27.8}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Public fair value is 5 × 8 × 0.62 = 24.8, the midpoint of the previous quote, and no new information has been revealed. My rough estimate of expected one-step profit favours an ask near 30.9 and a bid near 18–19, and the bid side is flat across that range. So I'll keep the same quotes.

{"bid": 18.7, "ask": 30.9}

**Fair value:** After flips 1 and 2 (both heads), the posterior on the coin is P(biased 0.8) ≈ 0.63. Flips 3–8 are not yet revealed, so the expected settlement is 5 × (2 + 6 × 0.689) ≈ **30.7**. The distribution of settlement values is 10, 15, …, 40 with probabilities of about 0.6%, 3.6%, 9.6%, 16.7%, 24.2%, 28.3%, 17.1%.

**Quoting:** Noise traders trade with the expected edge 0.8 × P(trade) × distance. That is maximised about 5 from fair value (≈ 6.6 × 0.75). Informed traders (20%) trade only when the true value is beyond my quote, which pushes both sides outward.

- **Bid:** Optimising the bid against the informed-trader loss puts it at a kink near 25.0 (V = 25 is indifferent at that point), with expected edge ≈ 0.70.
- **Ask:** The optimum is about 36.3–36.4. I'll quote 36.4, which rounds up cleanly. This side is also the one I want to hit, since I'm long 1.

Inventory doesn't shift the quotes. Position value is a martingale at fair value, and I'm well inside the ±3 limits.

{"bid": 25.0, "ask": 36.4}

**Fair value:** Flips 1 to 7 show 5 heads and 2 tails. The posterior is P(fair coin) ≈ 0.472 and P(biased coin) ≈ 0.528, so P(flip 8 = heads) ≈ 0.658. Flip 8 is never revealed before settlement, so the public fair value is 25 + 5 × 0.658 ≈ 28.29.

**Informed-trader risk:** The settlement value is either 25 (flip 8 tails) or 30 (flip 8 heads). An informed buyer takes our ask only if it is below 30. An informed seller hits our bid only if it is above 25. So an ask at or above 30 and a bid at or below 25 avoid adverse selection.

**Noise-only optima:**
- **Bid:** maximising 0.8 · Φ((b − 28.29)/6.6) · (28.29 − b) gives b ≈ 23.3. This is below 25, so no informed sells.
- **Ask:** maximising 0.8 · (1 − Φ((a − 28.29)/6.6)) · (a − 28.29) gives a ≈ 33.2. This is above 30, so no informed buys.

Inventory (+1) does not change the expected-profit optimum, so I quote the same spread. Rounding gives a bid of 23.3 (down) and an ask of 33.3 (up).

{"bid": 23.3, "ask": 33.3}

The coin posterior after flips 1-7 (five heads in seven flips) gives P(bias 0.8) ≈ 0.53. The expected total heads is 5 + 0.66 ≈ 5.66, so the public fair value is about 28.3. The settlement is 25 or 30.

The earlier trades don't change this estimate. An informed trader could never have bought at 33.3 or sold at 23.3 given the possible settlement values, so those trades came from noise traders.

For this last quote, expected profit on each side is maximised where the noise-trader term (roughly 0.8 × distance from fair value × probability of trade) peaks. That lands at about 5 points from fair value on each side, which gives a bid near 23.3 and an ask near 33.3. Neither price is in the range where the informed trader would trade profitably against me, so there's no extra adverse-selection term to adjust for.

{"bid": 23.3, "ask": 33.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Quote 1 has no revealed information, so the public fair value is the prior mean: 0.2·0.3 + 0.3·0.4 + 0.5·0.5 = 0.43 heads per flip, or 6 × 0.43 = 2.58 for settlement.

Each side is evaluated separately, since one counterparty trades on at most one side. Using the exact Binomial mixture for settlement S and the noise traders' N(2.58, 1.3²) valuations, the expected profit per quote is:

- **Ask A:** informed buyers take the ask when S > A, and noise buyers take it when their valuation exceeds A. The best multiple of 0.1 is about A = 4.0, with expected profit ≈ +0.06 per quote. A = 3.0 loses money, because informed buyers mostly arrive when S is high.
- **Bid B:** informed sellers hit the bid when S < B. The best multiple of 0.1 is about B = 1.0, with expected profit ≈ +0.066 per quote. B = 2.0 loses money for the same reason.

Quoting tight around 2.58 loses on the informed flow, so the spread needs to be wide. This is a one-step myopic optimum. Later quotes can adjust as flips are revealed and the trade history updates the public fair value.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.0}

Before any flips are revealed, the public fair value is E[heads] = 6 × (0.2×0.3 + 0.3×0.4 + 0.5×0.5) = 2.58. Informed traders buy from me whenever the settlement S exceeds my ask, and sell to me whenever S is below my bid. I priced the bid and ask separately against the settlement distribution, using the mixture of binomials and the noise traders' N(2.58, 1.3²) valuations. Under that model, the expected profit per quote is highest with a bid near 1.0 and an ask near 4.2. That is a wide quote, because adverse selection from informed traders is large while the true settlement distribution is spread out.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.2}

**Fair value:** Flip 1 was tails, so settlement equals heads in flips 2 to 6. Updating the coin prior on flip 1 gives E[p] ≈ 0.419, so the public fair value is about 5 × 0.419 ≈ 2.10.

**Adverse selection:** Informed traders know the settlement value S, so they hit my quote only when it is mispriced against them. Noise traders have valuations around 2.10 with sd 1.3. The expected profit from each side is 0.5 × (informed edge) + 0.5 × (noise edge). Using the posterior distribution of S, the one-quote optimum is roughly:
- Ask ≈ 3.65 (informed buying only when S ≥ 4, about 11.7% chance, while the noise trade probability is about 12%).
- Bid ≈ 0.82 (informed selling only when S = 0, about 8% chance).

Rounding to the 0.1 grid gives ask 3.7 (rounded up) and bid 0.8 (rounded down).

{"bid": 0.8, "ask": 3.7}

The trades so far suggest the settlement value is low. The two sales to me at 1.0 and 0.8 are consistent with informed sellers, who only sell when settlement is below the bid. Since flip 1 was tails, settlement is at most 5, and the posterior puts about 78% on zero heads in the remaining flips. My estimate of the fair value is roughly 0.6.

- **Bid 0:** Buying at 0 can't lose money, because settlement is never negative. Informed sellers never sell at 0, and noise sellers with valuation below 0 are the only source of trades. Any sale here earns the settlement value.
- **Ask 5:** Settlement is at most 5, so selling at 5 can't lose money either. Lower asks would mostly attract informed buyers when the settlement is high, which makes them unprofitable at this posterior.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 5.0}

Flips 1 to 5 are all tails, so settlement equals flip 6 (0 or 1). The posterior over the coin, using likelihoods 0.7^5, 0.6^5 and 0.5^5, is about 0.46, 0.32 and 0.22 for biases 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5. That gives P(flip 6 = heads) ≈ 0.375, which is the public fair value.

- **Ask at 1.0:** An informed buyer only trades when its valuation exceeds my ask. At 1.0 it never buys, since its valuation is at most 1. Noise traders still buy at 1.0 about 31% of the time, and each such trade is worth about 0.6 to me. Lowering the ask adds a few noise fills, but the informed buys on V=1 cost more than they gain.
- **Bid at 0:** An informed seller only trades when its valuation is below my bid. At 0 it never sells, since its valuation is at least 0. Noise traders still sell to me about 39% of the time, each worth about 0.375 in expectation. Raising the bid lets informed sellers hit me on V=0 at a loss.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.0}

**Setup:** Flips 1 to 5 were all tails, so settlement equals flip 6, V ∈ {0, 1}. Posterior on the coin after 5 tails: P(0.3) ≈ 0.46, P(0.4) ≈ 0.32, P(0.5) ≈ 0.22. So P(V=1) ≈ 0.375, and the public fair value is 0.375.

**Adverse selection:** An informed buyer hits my ask only if V=1 and ask<1. An informed seller hits my bid only if V=0 and bid>0. Quotes at or above 1 on the ask and at or below 0 on the bid therefore avoid informed flow entirely.

**Noise-trader optimisation:** Against noise traders (valuation ~ N(0.375, 1.3²)), expected profit from the ask is (a − 0.375)·P(noise buys at a)·0.5, which peaks near a ≈ 1.35, so I post 1.4. On the bid side, (0.375 − b)·P(noise sells at b)·0.5 peaks near b ≈ −0.6. Expected trade profit is about 0.11 on each side at these levels, compared with about 0.07 on the bid at 0.

I'm assuming negative bids are accepted, since the rules set no price floor. If they aren't, the fallback is bid 0.

{"bid": -0.6, "ask": 1.4}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value before any flips are revealed is 7 × 0.47 = 3.29. Since no trade occurred at quote 1 (bid 1, ask 5.5), the posterior shifts slightly lower, to about 3.24. The 20% informed-trader chance makes the extremes costly, so I'm keeping the spread roughly symmetric around that value, close to the previous quote. Rough expected-value checks put the ask near 5.5 (informed buyers are rare above that, and the noise-trader gain is largest there) and the bid near 1.0. Both sides come out at about +0.35 expected profit per quote.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 5.5}

Prior mean of p is 0.3(0.2) + 0.4(0.5) + 0.3(0.7) = 0.47, so the fair value of total heads is 7 × 0.47 = 3.29. I'm long one unit, so I'll lean toward selling. Informed traders make the wide spread (1 to 5.5) reasonable, and the ask near 5.2 keeps most of the expected edge while raising the chance of a sale. The bid stays at 1.0 so I don't add to the long position.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 5.2}

**Fair value.** Flip 1 = 1 is the only revealed flip. The posterior on the coin is about 0.13 / 0.43 / 0.45 for p = 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.7, so the posterior mean heads probability is about 0.55. The remaining six flips have expected heads of 6 × 0.55 ≈ 3.31, so the public fair value of settlement is about 1 + 3.31 ≈ **4.3**.

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement S = 1 + K, where K is the number of heads in flips 2–7. Its approximate probabilities are:

| S | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 0.04 | 0.09 | 0.16 | 0.23 | 0.25 | 0.18 | 0.06 |

**Trade history.** The quote-2 sale at bid 1 is best explained by a noise trader. Informed traders would only sell if S < 1, which is impossible now that flip 1 = 1. So it carries little information about the coin.

**Quote choice.** Noise traders value the contract at about N(4.3, 2.7). Informed traders (prob 0.2) trade against me when S is outside my quotes. Maximising expected per-trade profit gives:
- Ask: highest around 6.5 (about 0.36 expected profit), flat near 6.4–6.6.
- Bid: highest around 2.1 (about 0.35 expected profit), flat near 2.0–2.2.

The position is only +1, so I'm not shading the quotes much for inventory.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 6.5}

**Fair value:** Given flip 1 = heads, the posterior on the coin is about 0.13 / 0.43 / 0.45 for p = 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.7. The expected bias is about 0.551, so the expected settlement is 1 + 6 × 0.551 ≈ 4.31.

**Quote choice:** I computed the expected gain on each side against the counterparty model. Informed traders (20%) hit the quote only when the true value is beyond it. Noise traders (80%) trade with N(4.31, 2.7) valuations.
- **Ask:** the gain peaks at about 6.4 to 6.5 (≈0.36 per quote). Lower asks give up edge to noise buyers, and higher asks lose volume.
- **Bid:** the gain peaks at about 2.0 (≈0.354). Higher bids get picked off by informed sellers when the value is low.

Position +1 is well inside the ±3 limit, and at risk-neutral marking the held unit is still worth about 4.31, so I'm not skewing for inventory.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 6.4}

**Fair value:** Two heads so far (flips 1 and 2; flip 3 was tails). Updating the coin prior on flips H, H, T gives posterior weights of about 0.09 for p=0.2, 0.48 for p=0.5 and 0.43 for p=0.7, so the posterior mean of p is about 0.557. The expected heads in flips 4 to 7 is 4 × 0.557 ≈ 2.23, so the fair value is about 4.23. The settlement value is 2 + Binomial(4, p) mixed over the posterior, so it lies in [2, 6].

**Fair value:** Four heads are revealed, so the posterior on the coin is P(p=0.7) ≈ 0.85 and P(p=0.5) ≈ 0.15. The three unrevealed flips then give expected total heads ≈ 6.01, so the public fair value is about 60.1. The settlement can only be 40, 50, 60 or 70.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only lifts the ask when the settlement exceeds it. Since 70 is the maximum possible settlement, an ask at 70 gives informed traders nothing to exploit. It also keeps a good noise-trader edge, because noise buyers arrive about 18% of the time at that price. Among the asks I checked, 70 maximised expected profit.

**Bid:** Informed sellers hit the bid when the settlement is below it. A bid around 50 balances the noise-trader edge against the 4% chance the settlement is 40, and it came out slightly ahead of nearby bids.

{"bid": 50, "ask": 70}

**Posterior after flips 1-4 (all heads):** The coin is p=0.5 with posterior 0.148 and p=0.7 with posterior 0.852. The expected heads in the three unrevealed flips (5, 6, 7) is 2.01, so the fair value is about 10 × (4 + 2.01) ≈ 60.1.

**Settlement distribution:** Total heads is 4, 5, 6 or 7 with probabilities about 0.04, 0.22, 0.43 and 0.31, so the settlement value V is 40, 50, 60 or 70.

**Quote choice:** Noise traders value the contract at 60.1 with σ=11, and informed traders value it at V. Maximising expected per-quote profit on each side:
- **Ask:** Informed buyers appear only when V > ask, and V never exceeds 70, so an ask of 70 removes that loss. The expected edge peaks at 70.
- **Bid:** The best bid is about 50. Below 50, the spread gives up edge on noise sellers. Above 50, informed sellers at V = 40 or 50 add losses.

Position is 0, so there is no inventory skew. The ask of 70 and bid of 50 match the prior quote-5 spread, which drew no trades.

{"bid": 50, "ask": 70}

**Posterior:** Six straight heads favour the 0.7 coin. P(biased | data) ≈ 0.919, so P(flip 7 = heads) ≈ 0.684. The public fair value is 10 × (6 + 0.684) ≈ 66.8. Settlement is 70 if flip 7 is heads and 60 if tails.

**Adverse selection:** An informed counterparty buys from me only if settlement > my ask, and sells to me only if settlement < my bid. Since settlement is 60 or 70, a bid at or below 60 and an ask at or above 70 means informed traders never trade with me.

**Quote sizing:** Noise traders have valuation ~N(66.8, 11), independent of the true settlement, so their trades carry no information. Maximising expected profit over those trades:
- **Bid:** the expected gain is maximised near 58.5 (the marginal condition φ(z)(66.8 − b)/11 = Φ(z) holds there).
- **Ask:** the expected gain rises with the ask until roughly 75.

Both quotes stay clear of the informed traders' thresholds, so only noise traders can hit them.

{"bid": 58.5, "ask": 75}

Flips 1–6 are all heads, so the posterior on the biased coin is about 0.92. The public fair value of flip 7 is then about 0.684 heads, so the public fair settlement is 60 + 6.84 ≈ 66.84.

The settlement is either 60 (flip 7 tails) or 70 (flip 7 heads). An informed counterparty sells to my bid only when the settlement is 60, so the bid must be at or below 60 to avoid informed sales. It buys at my ask only when the settlement is 70, so the ask must be at or above 70. Within those bounds, the noise-trader fill probabilities set the best prices.

- **Bid:** the expected profit of buying at B is about 0.65·Φ((B−66.84)/11)·(66.84−B), which peaks near B ≈ 58.5 (about 1.22 per quote).
- **Ask:** the expected profit of selling at A is about 0.65·Φ((66.84−A)/11)·(A−66.84), which peaks near A ≈ 75 (about 1.22). Pricing just above 70 avoids informed buys, and the noise-trader term is larger at 75 than at 70.

Both are valid multiples of 0.1, and the position of 0 is well within limits. These are the same prices as quote 7, since the information set is unchanged.

{"bid": 58.5, "ask": 75}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Prior: P(heads) averages 0.62, so the fair value of the contract is 10 × 7 × 0.62 = **43.4**. Informed counterparties (35%) trade whenever the settlement value is on the wrong side of my quote, so I need a spread wide enough that the adverse-selection loss on informed trades is offset by the expected gain from noise traders.

Rough one-shot expected-profit estimates, using the exact distribution of the heads count under the coin mixture:
- Ask at 58: net expected profit ≈ +0.56 per unit from the ask side.
- Bid at 30: net expected profit ≈ +0.49 from the bid side.

Quotes closer to 43.4 lose money to informed flow. These estimates ignore how trade history will update the fair value, so treat them as a first-quote baseline.

{"bid": 30.0, "ask": 58.0}

With no new information revealed, the public fair value is 10 × 7 × 0.62 = 43.4. Settlement is 10 × heads, so it takes values 0, 10, ..., 70, and the informed trader's valuation is that exact value.

I estimated expected profit per side as a function of quote. On the ask side, a sale at 57 gives about 0.54 expected profit per quote, and 58 gives about 0.54 as well. On the bid side, 30 gives about 0.49, the best of the prices I checked (31 gives about 0.47, 29 about 0.44). Both sides are close to flat across nearby prices, so these estimates are rough.

I'll quote bid 30 and ask 57.

{"bid": 30, "ask": 57}

**Quote 3: bid 35, ask 57**

Posterior on the coin after flips 1–3 (0, 1, 1): P(p=0.7) ≈ 0.64, P(p=0.5) ≈ 0.36. Total heads so far are 2, and the remaining 4 flips add X heads. The expected settlement is 10 × (2 + 4 × 0.63) ≈ 45.1.

The distribution of settlement V = 10 × (2 + X) is roughly: 20 (2.8%), 30 (13.9%), 40 (30.5%), 50 (35.3%), 60 (17.6%).

Using a one-shot model with 35% informed and 65% noise traders (noise valuation ~ N(45.1, 11)), expected profit is highest near an ask of about 56 and a bid of about 34. Profit is flat over a few cents either way, so I skew the quote slightly toward buying, since I am already short 1. I set the bid at 35 and the ask at 57, which makes it a little less attractive to sell to me.

{"bid": 35, "ask": 57}

**Posterior after the trades so far**

- Flips 1-3 (0,1,1) give P(fair) ≈ 0.36 and P(biased) ≈ 0.64. Known heads = 2, so total heads H = 2 + (heads in flips 4-7).
- Both 57 buys are informative. An informed buyer at 57 means V > 57, which requires H = 6 (flips 4-7 all heads). Noise buyers at 57 are plausible, but the informed component pushes the posterior toward H = 6.
- Rough posterior: P(H=6) ≈ 0.74. The remaining mass is spread over H = 2..5, with E[H | H ≤ 5] ≈ 4.2.
- Public fair value ≈ 10 × 5.53 ≈ 55.3.

**Quote 4**

- Ask: an ask at 57 to 59 is negative or marginal, because informed traders buy when V = 60. An ask of 60 or higher avoids informed buyers entirely, since V is at most 60. Expected edge from noise buyers peaks around 63-64, so I'm asking 64.
- Bid: informed sellers hit the bid when V is 20-40. Expected edge from noise sellers, net of that adverse selection, peaks around 44.5-45, so I'm bidding 44.5.

These are rough, myopic estimates. The posterior is sensitive to how much weight I put on the 57 buys as informed signals.

{"bid": 44.5, "ask": 64.0}

**Belief update:** Flips 1–4 show 3 heads and 1 tail. The likelihood is 0.5⁴ = 0.0625 for the fair coin and 0.7³·0.3 = 0.1029 for the 0.7 coin. Weighting by the 2/5 and 3/5 priors gives P(fair) ≈ 0.29 and P(0.7) ≈ 0.71.

**Settlement distribution:** Flips 5–7 are unknown. Their expected heads are about 1.93, so the expected total is about 4.93 heads and the fair value is about 49.3. The possible settlement values are 30 (≈5.5%), 40 (≈24%), 50 (≈42%) and 60 (≈28%).

**Quotes:** Taking the expected profit per side, with the noise trader's valuation distributed N(49.3, 11) and the informed trader trading whenever V is past my price:
- **Ask:** 60 maximises expected profit. Above 60 the noise-trader fill probability falls faster than the margin rises, and at 60 the informed trader does not buy because V = 60 is not strictly above the ask.
- **Bid:** 40 maximises expected profit. Below 40 I lose too many noise fills, and above 40 the informed trader selling at V = 30 or V = 40 costs more than the extra fills gain.

I'm not adjusting for the −2 position, since at settlement inventory only matters through its expected value, which is already in the fair value.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 60}

**Posterior and value.** Flips 1–4 show 3 heads in 4 flips. The likelihood is 1/16 under p=0.5 and 0.343·0.3 ≈ 0.103 under p=0.7. With prior weights 0.4 and 0.6, the posterior is P(p=0.7) ≈ 0.71 and P(p=0.5) ≈ 0.29.

Three flips (5, 6, 7) remain. Their expected heads are about 1.93, so the public fair value is 10·(3 + 1.93) ≈ 49.3. The settlement value V is one of 30, 40, 50, 60, with probabilities about 0.06, 0.24, 0.42, 0.28.

**Ask at 60.** An informed buyer needs V > 60, which is impossible, so only noise traders buy here. Expected profit per quote is about +1.15 at 60, and it is slightly lower at 59 or 61. Quoting 60 exactly also means an informed trader with V = 60 does not trade.

**Bid at 40.** An informed seller hits this only if V = 30 (V = 40 is not below 40). Expected profit per quote is about +1.01 at 40, and it falls off sharply at 41 and above, where the V = 40 informed sellers start trading.

The position is −2, so both sides remain available.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 60}

**Estimate of the settlement value.** The six revealed flips show 5 heads. The posterior on the biased coin (P=0.7) is about 0.83, so P(flip 7 = heads) ≈ 0.67. The public fair value is 10 × (5 + 0.67) ≈ 56.7. The settlement is either 50 (flip 7 tails) or 60 (heads).

**Adverse selection.** Informed counterparties only trade when the settlement value is on the far side of our price. An informed buyer can only hit an ask below 60, and an informed seller can only hit a bid above 50. Pricing the ask above 60 and the bid at or below 50 removes the informed risk and leaves only noise-trader flow.

**Expected edge per side (noise traders only):**
- Ask 65: a noise buyer arrives with probability about 0.22, earning about 8.3 over fair value. Expected edge ≈ 1.22.
- Bid 48: a noise seller arrives with probability about 0.22, earning about 8.7 under fair value. Expected edge ≈ 1.21.

Both quotes sit near the edge-maximising point on their side. Neither side can be hit by an informed trader, so the quote is roughly as good as the noise-trader model allows.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 65}

**Posterior:** Flips 1–6 show 5 heads and 1 tail. The likelihood ratio favours the 0.7 coin, giving P(biased) ≈ 0.83. So P(flip 7 = heads) ≈ 0.67, and the settlement is 50 or 60 with probabilities about 0.33 and 0.67. The public fair value is about 56.7.

**Ask:** Noise buyers take the ask with probability Φ((56.7 − A)/11). Informed buyers only take it when A < 60, and that case is unprofitable for me. Expected profit peaks near A ≈ 65.

**Bid:** Noise sellers hit the bid with probability Φ((B − 56.7)/11). Informed sellers only hit it when B > 50, and that case is unprofitable for me. Expected profit peaks near B ≈ 48.

The two sides are independent because only one counterparty arrives, so I quote the best price on each side.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 65}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 7/10, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value before any reveals is 5 × 6 × 0.56 = 16.8, since each flip has expected heads 0.7×0.5 + 0.3×0.7 = 0.56. Against informed traders, who know the settlement value S, the best quotes sit where the expected profit from trades is highest. Weighting informed and noise flow equally, that is about 25.5 for the ask and about 7.1 for the bid. Nothing has been revealed and the quotes are unchanged, so I'll keep them at that level.

{"bid": 7.1, "ask": 25.5}

**Quote 4 (stage 2):** Posterior on the coin given flip 1 = heads is P(fair) = 0.625, P(biased) = 0.375. The expected settlement is 5 × (1 + 5 × 0.575) = 19.375. The remaining heads count has a discrete distribution, so settlement V is 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30. I chose the bid and ask that maximise expected profit against a 50/50 mix of informed and noise counterparties. That gives a bid near 10 and an ask near 29.3, about 9.5 either side of fair value. Position is flat, so no inventory adjustment is needed.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 29.3}

**Quote 6: bid 10, ask 29.2**

- **Posterior:** Flip 1 was heads, so P(biased coin) = 0.21/0.56 = 0.375. Expected heads in flips 2–6 is 2.875, so the public fair value of settlement is 5 × (1 + 2.875) ≈ 19.4.
- **Settlement distribution:** S ∈ {5, 10, …, 30}, with P(S=5..30) ≈ 0.020, 0.108, 0.245, 0.311, 0.233, 0.083.
- **Ask:** Noise-buyer edge (A − 19.4) against informed buying when S > A. The optimum is near 29.2–29.3, where the only informed buys are at S = 30. The objective is essentially flat there, so I pick 29.2.
- **Bid:** The mirror-image trade-off with informed selling when S < B gives a kink optimum at 10. Above 10 the informed-sell cost rises sharply, and below 10 the noise-seller gain falls off.

This is a one-shot optimum that ignores the inventory and reveal dynamics for the remaining quotes.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 29.2}

**Fair value:** Three of the four revealed flips are heads, so the coin posterior is P(fair) ≈ 0.586 and P(biased) ≈ 0.414. The unrevealed flips 5 and 6 then give an expected 1.17 further heads, so the expected settlement is about 5 × 4.17 ≈ 20.8.

**Settlement support:** Total heads is 3 + X with X ∈ {0, 1, 2}, so settlement is 15, 20 or 25. Informed counterparties trade only when settlement is beyond my quote. If my ask is above 25 and my bid is at or below 15, informed traders never trade against me, and only noise traders (valuation ~ N(20.8, 9.9)) do.

**Optimal quotes:** Within those bounds, each side maximises P(noise trade) × edge. The first-order condition gives a distance of about 0.75σ ≈ 7.45 from fair value on each side:
- Ask ≈ 20.8 + 7.45 ≈ 28.3
- Bid ≈ 20.8 − 7.45 ≈ 13.4, rounded down to 13.3

This is a small but positive expected edge per quote. The position is flat and the limits are unlikely to bind with 3 quotes left, so I'm not adjusting for inventory.

{"bid": 13.3, "ask": 28.3}

**Quote 8: bid 13.3, ask 28.3.** This matches the previous quote, since the posterior hasn't changed.

- **Posterior:** Flips 1 to 4 show 3 heads, so the fair coin has posterior 0.586 and the biased coin 0.414. Expected heads per remaining flip is 0.583.
- **Fair value:** The public fair value is 5 × (3 + 2 × 0.583) ≈ 20.83.
- **Settlement support:** Flips 5 and 6 can only give 0, 1 or 2 heads, so settlement is 15, 20 or 25. The informed counterparty can therefore never buy at 28.3 or sell at 13.3.
- **Noise-trader optimum:** With σ = 9.9, the expected profit per side is maximised where the distance from fair value is about 0.75σ ≈ 7.4. That gives a bid near 13.4 (rounded down to 13.3) and an ask near 28.3 (rounded up to 28.3).

{"bid": 13.3, "ask": 28.3}

The coin is fair with posterior probability about 0.586 after the 3 heads in 4 revealed flips. The settlement is 5 × (3 + heads in flips 5–6), so it takes one of three values: 15 (≈0.18), 20 (≈0.47), or 25 (≈0.35). The public fair value is about 20.83.

Since this is the last quote, inventory doesn't matter. The informed counterparty trades only when its valuation is on the wrong side of my price, so it only costs me. Noise traders trade regardless of the settlement, so they are the source of profit. Optimising each side against that gives:

- **Ask:** the best ask is above 25, where the informed trader never buys. The noise-only optimum is about 28.26, which rounds up to **28.3**.
- **Bid:** the best bid is below 15, where the informed trader never sells. The noise-only optimum is about 13.39, which rounds down to **13.3**.

Both sides have positive expected edge, so I quote both. At most one trade can occur.

{"bid": 13.3, "ask": 28.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 7/10, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
With no revealed flips, the public fair value is 5 × 6 × 0.56 = 16.8. Noise traders trade at roughly fair value ± 9.9, and informed traders trade against us whenever the settlement value lies beyond our quote. Because the noise is large, the expected-profit-maximising quotes sit well away from fair value: about 25.5 on the ask and 7 on the bid. I'm estimating these by hand, not by exact computation.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 25.5}

Quote 3 is the last quote before the flip 1 reveal, so no hidden information is available yet. The two empty rounds at bid 7 and ask 25.5 slightly raise the estimated fair value to about 17.1. Against that fair value, I checked the expected profit on each side across the informed and noise counterparties. Expected profit peaks near an ask of 25 and a bid of 9, and both quotes are slightly tighter than the previous ones, which should bring in more flow.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 25.0}

**Quote 4: bid 10, ask 29**

- **Fair value:** Flip 1 = heads gives P(fair coin) = 0.625 and P(biased) = 0.375, so the expected settlement is about 19.4. The earlier buy at 25 suggests a high value, nudging the public fair value to roughly 19.5.
- **Settlement distribution:** Settlement is 5 × (1 + heads in flips 2–6), so it lies in {5, 10, …, 30}, with about a 9% chance of 30.
- **Ask:** Noise buyers come in at prices well above fair value, and informed buyers only take the ask when the value is near 30. The expected profit from the ask side peaks around 28–30. I chose 29.
- **Bid:** Symmetrically, the expected profit from the bid side peaks around 10.
- **Inventory:** Position (-1) is well inside the limits and doesn't change expected profit, so I quoted purely on expected value.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 29}

**Quote 5: bid 10, ask 29**

Flip 1 was heads, so the coin posterior is P(fair) = 0.625 and P(biased) = 0.375. The public fair value of the settlement is about 5 × (1 + 5 × 0.575) ≈ 19.4.

Expected profit on each side, after adverse selection from informed traders and noise-trader flow:
- **Ask:** the edge is maximised around 29–30. At 29 it is about 0.755, and at 30 about 0.753.
- **Bid:** the edge is maximised at 10, about 0.754. Neighbouring bids (9.5, 10.5, 11) are slightly worse.

Position is -1, which is well inside the ±5 limits. Settlement-expected profit is linear in the position, so inventory does not change the choice.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 29}

**Quote 6: bid 10, ask 26.6**

Before stage 2 only flip 1 is public, but the trade history also moves the public fair value. Quote 3's buy at 25 and the no-trades at 29 and 25.5 shift the posterior. Roughly, the coin posterior gives a fair value of about 18.9, down from 19.4 before the history.

The posterior over the settlement value (in units of 5 × heads) is about: 5 → 0.1%, 10 → 12%, 15 → 27%, 20 → 34%, 25 → 26%, 30 → 1.3%.

- **Ask:** an informed buyer only takes the ask if the settlement value is 30, which is now unlikely. Noise buyers arrive with a probability that falls as the ask rises. Expected profit peaks near 26.5–26.7, so I'm quoting 26.6.
- **Bid:** near 10, informed sellers only appear with value 5 (very unlikely), and noise sellers are worth buying from at 10 against a fair value near 18.9. Expected profit peaks at 10.

These estimates are approximate, since I simplified the noise-trader fair values at earlier quotes. My position of -1 doesn't change the expected-value calculation, so I've ignored it.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 26.6}

**Posterior.** Flips 1–4 show 2 heads in 4. The fair coin (prior 0.7) has likelihood 1/16 and the biased coin (prior 0.3) has likelihood 0.0441, so P(fair) ≈ 0.768 and P(biased) ≈ 0.232.

**Settlement.** Total heads will be 2 + (heads in flips 5–6), so the settlement value is 10, 15 or 20 with probabilities about 0.213, 0.481 and 0.306. The expected value is μ ≈ 15.46, which is also the public fair value.

**Quotes.** Informed counterparties only trade when the value is past my price, which costs me edge. Noise traders trade with probability P(N > ask) or P(N < bid) with N ~ N(15.46, 9.9²), and each trade earns the distance from μ.

- Ask: setting it at or above 20 means informed traders never buy. The edge is maximised at μ + 0.75·9.9 ≈ 22.9.
- Bid: setting it at or below 10 means informed traders never sell. The edge is maximised at μ − 0.75·9.9 ≈ 8.0.

Both sides earn about 0.84 expected edge per quote. The position of −1 is well inside the ±5 limits, so it doesn't change the choice.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 22.9}

game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 5 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value is 5 × 5 × E[p] = 25 × 0.70 = **17.5**, since E[p] = 0.2(0.2) + 0.3(0.7) + 0.5(0.9) = 0.70. Noise traders value the contract around 17.5 with sd 12, and informed traders know the exact value (0 to 25 in steps of 5). The noise-trader spread alone would be about ±9, but informed flow adds adverse selection, so the optimal quotes are slightly asymmetric: the bid moves down (informed sellers are concentrated at V = 0 and 5) and the ask stays near 26.5.

{"bid": 7.3, "ask": 26.6}

Nothing new is revealed, so the public fair value is still the prior mean: E[heads] = 5 × 0.70 = 3.5, giving an expected settlement of 17.5. Informed traders can only buy above 25 (the maximum settlement) and only sell below 0, so there's no adverse selection on either side at these prices. The informed traders can't profitably hit a quote at 26.5 or a bid at 7.3, and the noise traders' flow is priced against 17.5. Expected profit is about 1.6 per side. This is the same reasoning as quote 1, and the optimum is nearly flat around these levels.

{"bid": 7.3, "ask": 26.5}

**Quote 4: bid 12.0, ask 30.5**

- **Fair value:** After flip 1 = heads, the posterior mean of the heads in flips 2–5 is 3.2, so the expected settlement is 5 × (1 + 3.2) = 21.0. The three earlier no-trade outcomes are also informative: an informed counterparty would have traded unless the settlement value fell inside each quoted spread. Updating on that pushes the fair value to about 21.4.
- **Ask:** Above 25 the informed counterparty can never buy profitably, so only noise-trader adverse selection matters. Maximising (A − 21.4) × P(noise buys) gives an ask near 30.4–30.5.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers at a bid of about 12 only arrive when the settlement is 5 or 10, which has probability about 0.048. Balancing that against noise-trader sales gives a bid near 12.0.

{"bid": 12.0, "ask": 30.5}

**Fair value.** After flips 1 and 2 are both heads, the posterior on the coin is about 0.014 (p=0.2), 0.263 (p=0.7) and 0.723 (p=0.9). The expected bias is about 0.8375, so the expected heads in flips 3-5 is about 2.51. The expected settlement is 5 × (2 + 2.51) ≈ 22.56.

**Adverse selection.** Settlement is a multiple of 5 in {10, 15, 20, 25}, with P(25) ≈ 0.62. An informed buyer would hit an ask below 25, so a high ask is safer. The noise-trader spread is 12, so to maximise expected profit I set the ask near where the marginal sale profit is zero. That gives about 31.6, which is above 25 so informed traders never buy from it. The same logic on the bid gives about 13.4, where informed sellers only arrive if settlement is 10, a small loss.

Expected profit per side is about 1.6 per quote.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 31.6}

**Fair value:** Flips 1 and 2 were both heads, so the coin posterior is about 0.014 (p=0.2), 0.263 (p=0.7) and 0.723 (p=0.9). The expected number of heads in the three unrevealed flips is 2.51, so the expected settlement is 5 × (2 + 2.51) ≈ 22.56. Settlement can only take the values 10, 15, 20 or 25.

**Ask:** Informed buyers only buy when the settlement value exceeds my ask. Since the value never exceeds 25, an ask above 25 faces no informed flow. Above 25, the expected profit from noise traders is maximised near 22.56 + 0.75 × 12 ≈ 31.6.

**Bid:** The noise-only optimum is near 22.56 − 0.75 × 12 ≈ 13.5. Informed sellers arrive only when the value is 10, which pushes the bid slightly lower. The expected profit is essentially flat between 13.4 and 13.5, so I'll take 13.4.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 31.6}

Flips 1 to 4 are all heads, so the posterior over coins weights the p=0.9 coin most heavily. The expected flip-5 probability is about 0.863, so the fair settlement value is about 5 × (4 + 0.863) ≈ 24.3.

Settlement can only be 20 (flip 5 tails) or 25 (flip 5 heads). That creates no adverse-selection risk if I stay outside those values:
- An informed buyer hits my ask only if it is below 25, so an ask of 25 or higher avoids informed buys.
- An informed seller hits my bid only if it is above 20, so a bid of 20 or lower avoids informed sells.

Within those limits, I pick the quotes that maximise expected noise-trader profit. Noise traders have valuations around 24.3 with standard deviation 12. The optimal bid is about 15.3 and the optimal ask is about 33.3. Rounding gives bid 15.3 (rounds down) and ask 33.4 (rounds up).

{"bid": 15.3, "ask": 33.4}
