I then chose each side to maximise expected profit against the mixture: 80% noise traders with valuation ~N(2.36, 1.6²), and 20% informed traders who know the settlement value S, where S follows the mixture of Binomial(5, 0.4) and Binomial(5, 0.8).

- **Ask:** the optimum is about 3.78, which rounds up to 3.8. Informed buyers then trade only when S ≥ 4.
- **Bid:** the optimum sits at the kink at 1.0. Informed sellers trade only when S = 0, so S = 1 does not trade at this bid.

The current short position doesn't change the marginal analysis, since it is already reflected in the trade-by-trade profit at settlement.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 3.8}

Flip 1 was tails, so the posterior on the coin is P(p=0.4) = 9/11 and P(p=0.8) = 2/11. The public fair value of the settlement is about 2.36. I computed each side's expected edge, treating noise traders as arriving around the fair value and informed traders as trading whenever the true settlement is beyond my price.

- **Ask:** the best expected edge is near 3.8 (about 0.19 per quote). Lower asks are negative after adjusting for informed buyers.
- **Bid:** the best expected edge is near 1.0 (about 0.20 per quote), where informed sellers are rare because the settlement is unlikely to be below 1.

Position is 0, so both sides are open.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 3.8}

**Posterior after flips 1–4 (all tails):** Coin A (p=0.4) has posterior ≈ 0.992 and coin B (p=0.8) ≈ 0.008. Settlement = flips 5 + 6, so the public fair value is μ ≈ 0.81. The informed trader knows V ∈ {0, 1, 2} with P ≈ (0.357, 0.479, 0.164).

**Ask:** A buyer hits my ask when it is above the ask. Noise buyers pay roughly μ on average, and informed buyers take the ask only when V > a. Expected contribution is about 0.217 at a = 2.0, 0.213 at 1.9 and 0.217 at 2.1. Above 2.0 no informed trader can hit the ask, and the noise term is maximised near a ≈ 2.0. So the ask is 2.0.

**Bid:** A seller hits my bid when its valuation is below the bid. Noise sellers give me μ − b on average, and informed sellers never sell when V ≥ 0 and b ≤ 0. Expected contribution is about 0.218 at b = −0.4, 0.217 at −0.3 and 0.217 at −0.5. The optimum is near b ≈ −0.4. Bid 0 would give about 0.198, so the negative bid adds only a small amount.

The rules set no floor on prices, so a negative bid is allowed. If negative quotes are not wanted in practice, use bid 0 instead.

{"bid": -0.4, "ask": 2.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 5 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The public fair value is 17.5: each flip is heads with probability 0.7 on average, so E[settlement] = 5 × 5 × 0.7 = 17.5.

The settlement distribution is skewed toward high values (P(25) ≈ 0.35, P(20) ≈ 0.27, P(0) ≈ 0.07). Informed traders buy from me only when value exceeds my ask and sell to me only when value is below my bid. Working through expected profit per side, with noise traders at 17.5 ± 12 and informed traders at probability 0.2:

- **Ask side:** Profit ≈ 0.8·P(noise > A)·(A − 17.5) − 0.2·E[(V − A)⁺]. At A ≈ 18.5 this is slightly negative because of adverse selection. It peaks around A ≈ 26–27, where informed traders can no longer profitably buy (V ≤ 25). At 26.5 the expected profit is about 1.6.
- **Bid side:** Profit ≈ 0.8·P(noise < B)·(17.5 − B) − 0.2·E[(B − V)⁺]. The optimum is flat between about 7 and 8. At 7.5 the expected profit is about 1.5.

These quotes are wide, but under this model that is what maximises expected profit. I'll tighten as flips are revealed and the fair value moves.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 26.5}

**Fair value.** Flip 1 = tails updates the coin posterior to about (0.533, 0.300, 0.167) over the biases (0.2, 0.7, 0.9). That gives E[p] ≈ 0.467 and a fair settlement of 20 × 0.467 ≈ 9.33, which matches the midpoint of the previous quote.

**Settlement distribution.** Given flip 1 = 0, the settlement V = 5 × (heads in flips 2–5) takes values 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 with probabilities about 0.221, 0.242, 0.169, 0.186, 0.182.

**Quote analysis (one-period, risk-neutral).**
- Noise traders have σ = 12, so their trade probability falls slowly with distance from fair value. Each extra unit of spread earns little from them.
- Informed traders are the real cost. An ask below 20 gets hit when V = 20. A bid above 0 gets hit when V = 0.
- At ask = 20, no informed trader buys (V > 20 is impossible). Expected profit from the ask side is about 0.8 × 0.187 × 10.7 ≈ 1.6. Lower asks lose more to informed buyers than they gain in noise flow.
- At bid = 0, no informed trader sells (V < 0 is impossible). Expected profit from the bid side is about 0.8 × 0.218 × 9.3 ≈ 1.6. Higher bids add informed losses faster than noise gains.

This puts the optimum at bid 0 and ask 20, which is much wider than the previous 5.3/13.3. The model is myopic, so it ignores learning from later flips and inventory effects, but for this quote the wide, informed-proof quote is the better choice.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 20}

**Quote 5:** bid 0, ask 14.

**Public fair value.** Two tails so far, so the coin posterior is about 0.80 / 0.17 / 0.03 over biases 0.2 / 0.7 / 0.9, giving E[p] ≈ 0.306. With three unrevealed flips, the fair value of the contract is 5 × 3 × 0.306 ≈ 4.59.

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement is 5 × (heads in flips 3–5), so it takes values 0, 5, 10, 15 with probabilities about 0.41, 0.34, 0.16, 0.09.

**Ask.** Noise buyers are uninformative, so my expected profit per unit sold at ask A is roughly 0.8·P(V > A)·(A − 4.59), minus 0.2·E[(S − A)⁺] from informed buyers. This is maximised near A ≈ 14, with expected profit about 1.6 per quote. Quoting 13.5–14 is nearly as good.

**Bid.** The same logic on the sell side favours a bid below zero (around −4), since a low bid rarely trades but earns a lot per unit when it does. I quote 0 instead because negative prices fall outside the range seen so far and might be rejected. At 0 there are no informed sellers, and the expected profit is about 1.3 per quote, close to the best non-negative choice.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 14}

**Quote 6: bid 0, ask 14**

Flips 1 and 2 were both tails, so the posterior over coins is about 0.80 (p=0.2), 0.17 (p=0.7), 0.03 (p=0.9). The expected heads in the three unseen flips is about 0.92, so the fair value is about 4.6. Settlement is 0, 5, 10 or 15.

- **Ask at 14:** A noise trader buys with probability about 0.22 (valuation above 14), earning about 9.4 each. The informed buyer only trades when settlement is 15, costing about 0.02 in expectation. This is close to the best ask.
- **Bid at 0:** Settlement cannot be below 0, so an informed seller never trades here, and only noise sellers can hit it. Lower bids earn more per noise trade, and 0 is the floor I've used before.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 14}

**Quote 7 reasoning (brief):**

- Heads so far: 2. Settlement = 10 + 5·(flip 5), so V is 10 or 15.
- Posterior on the coin after flips 1–4 gives P(flip 5 = 1) ≈ 0.62. Quote 3's no-trade (ask 13.3) is mildly evidence for V = 10, so P(V = 15) ≈ 0.46 and the public fair value is about 12.3.
- Informed traders only trade if V is above my ask or below my bid, so a bid near 3 and an ask near 21 are outside their reach. Any fill there comes from noise traders.
- Noise traders have sd 12, so the expected profit per side, (a − μ)·P(buy) on the ask and (μ − b)·P(sell) on the bid, is maximised about 9 away from μ on each side. That gives an ask near 21.3 and a bid near 3.3.
- I'm long 2, which doesn't change the expected value of a risk-neutral position, so I quote both sides.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 21.4}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
**Quote 1: bid 2.0, ask 4.9**

Before any reveals, the public fair value is the prior expected total heads: 6 × (0.6 × 0.4 + 0.4 × 0.8) = 3.36. The settlement value V is the total heads count, with distribution P(V=0..6) ≈ 0.028, 0.113, 0.193, 0.199, 0.181, 0.179, 0.107.

Each side trades off two effects:
- **Noise traders** (80%) pay a spread edge when they trade, with valuation ~ N(3.36, 1.6).
- **Informed traders** (20%) know V and trade only when it is against me. Their expected loss on the ask is E[(V − a)⁺] and on the bid is E[(b − V)⁺].

Maximising expected profit on each side:
- **Ask:** the optimum is about 4.89, inside the (4, 5) band where P(V > a) = 0.287. Asks round up, so 4.9.
- **Bid:** the informed loss jumps at integers because V is integer-valued. The optimum sits at the integer 2.0, just before the slope rises.

Both sides are sensible, with bid < ask and an expected profit of roughly 0.36 per quote under this model.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 4.9}

**Fair value:** Flip 1 = heads gives a posterior of 3/7 on the 0.4 coin and 4/7 on the 0.8 coin. The expected total is 1 + 5 × 0.629 ≈ **4.14**. The settlement S ∈ {1,…,6} has distribution roughly {0.034, 0.115, 0.177, 0.216, 0.267, 0.192}.

**Ask:** Selling at A earns 0.8·P(V>A)·(A − 4.14) from noise traders, minus 0.2·Σ_{S>A} P(S)(S − A) from informed buyers. This is about 0.196 at A = 5.5, 0.196 at 5.6, and 0.194 at 5.4, so 5.5 is near optimal.

**Bid:** Buying at B earns 0.8·P(V<B)·(4.14 − B) from noise sellers, minus 0.2·Σ_{S<B} P(S)(B − S) from informed sellers. This is about 0.185 at B = 2.8, 0.185 at 2.7, and 0.181 at 2.9, so 2.8 is near optimal.

Expected profit is linear in position, so the +1 inventory doesn't change the per-quote optimum. The quote is wide because 20% of counterparties are informed and the noise sd is 1.6.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 5.5}

Flip 1 = heads gives posterior coin weights 3/7 (p=0.4) and 4/7 (p=0.8). The earlier trades also carry information: the sale at bid 2 suggests a low settlement, and the purchase at ask 5.5 suggests a high one. Combining these gives a settlement fair value of about 4.2. Quoting myopically to maximise expected profit against the noise traders (sd 1.6) and informed flow (20%) gives a bid near 2.9 and an ask near 5.8. Position is 0, so both sides are open.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 5.8}

Posterior on the coin after flips 1–4 (three heads, one tail): P(p=0.4) = 0.36, P(p=0.8) = 0.64. Flips 5 and 6 are unknown, so the settlement value is V = 3 + S, with P(V=3) ≈ 0.155, P(V=4) ≈ 0.378, P(V=5) ≈ 0.467. The fair value is E[V] ≈ 4.31.

Informed counterparties (20%) trade against us whenever V is on the far side of our quote. Noise traders (80%) are centred on 4.31 with sd 1.6, so they carry no adverse selection, only edge if the quote is away from fair value.

- **Ask:** Any ask at or above 5 is never hit by an informed buyer, since V ≤ 5. Among those, the noise-trader edge is largest near 5.5, so the ask is 5.5.
- **Bid:** A bid at 3.0 is never hit by an informed seller, since V ≥ 3. Moving the bid up to 3.1 gains a little from noise sellers but costs more from informed sellers, so the bid is 3.0.

I'm holding a long position of +1, but at fair value inventory doesn't change expected profit, so it doesn't change these quotes.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.5}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The public fair value is E[R] = 5, since R is uniform on 0 to 10. Each side can be treated separately, because a counterparty trades on only one side.

For the ask at price a, the informed trader buys when R > a, which costs me. The noise trader buys when its valuation exceeds a, with probability 0.65 × P(N(5, 2.4²) > a), and that trade earns a − 5 in expectation. Evaluating the expected profit per quote:

- a = 6.5: about 0.00
- a = 7.5: about +0.10
- a = 8.0: about +0.11
- a = 8.5: about +0.10

The optimum is near 8.0. By symmetry the bid is near 2.0, which also gives about +0.11. Both prices are multiples of 0.1, so no rounding is needed.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

Posterior after draw 1 = 0 is proportional to (10 − R). The quote-1 buy at 8 and the quote-2 no-trade at 4.2/10 both update it further: the buy at 8 implies R ≥ 9 for an informed buyer, and the no-trade at 4.2/10 implies R ∈ {5,…,9} for an informed trader. The resulting public fair value is about 4.6, with a wide spread of plausible values.

Because the counterparty is only ever one trader, the expected profit splits into an ask-side term and a bid-side term. Each one is maximised separately:
- **Ask:** the best sale price is about 7.5. Informed buyers (R ≥ 9 mostly) make higher asks costly, but noise buyers still pay above fair value.
- **Bid:** the best purchase price is about 1.8. Informed sellers (R low) make lower bids costly, and noise sellers provide the edge.

Both sides earn roughly +0.12 expected profit per trade at these prices, and position −1 is well within limits.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 7.5}

Quote 4 is the second stage-2 quote, and I'm flat (position 0).

**Posterior on red count R:** The draw-1 blue reveal gives weights (10 − R). The trades so far then shift it:
- Quote 1: a buy at ask 8 means the trader valued it above 8, which points to high R.
- Quote 2: no trade at bid 4.2 / ask 10 means the trader valued it between 4.2 and 10, which points to mid-to-high R.
- Quote 3: a sell at bid 1.8 means the trader valued it below 1.8, which points to low R.

Working through the Bayesian updates for the informed and noise-trader likelihoods gives a public fair value of about **2.5**. The posterior has about 0.6 mass on R ∈ {0, 1}, with about 0.2 on R ∈ {6, …, 9}.

**Bid side:** Informed sellers arrive only when R < bid. A bid of 0 means no informed seller ever trades with me, while noise sellers (valuation below 0) still arrive with probability about 0.15. The expected profit is about +0.24 per quote. Raising the bid above 0 adds informed sells (mostly R = 0) faster than it adds noise sells, so the bid should be 0.

**Ask side:** Informed buyers arrive when R > ask, and noise buyers when their valuation exceeds the ask. Expected profit peaks around an ask of 5 (about +0.065 per quote). Lower asks get hit by informed buyers with R ∈ {6, …, 9} and sell below fair value. Higher asks lose the noise buyers.

Both sides are roughly additive because a single counterparty trades at most one side. The bid is my most profitable side, and the ask is a small positive-expectation side.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 5.0}

**Fair value:** The draws give a posterior over red count K proportional to k(10-k), so the prior-plus-draws mean is 5. The quote history shifts this: the buy at 8 (quote 1) favours high K, the sell at 1.8 (quote 3) favours low K, and the buy at 5 (quote 4) favours high K. Combining these with draw 1 = blue and draw 2 = red gives a posterior mean of about 7.2. Most of the mass sits at K = 6 to 9, and K = 10 is ruled out because draw 1 was blue.

**Ask:** An informed buyer takes my ask only if K > ask. K = 10 has zero posterior probability, so an ask of 9.0 avoids informed buyers entirely. Noise buyers at 9.0 are a little over 1.7 above fair value, which gives positive expected edge (about +0.27 per unit of expected profit). Asks below 9 would invite informed buyers at K = 9, which has about 41% posterior probability, and turn the expected edge negative.

**Bid:** An informed seller takes my bid only if K < bid. At 5.0 that means K = 1 to 4, roughly 10% of the posterior. Among bids, 5.0 maximises expected edge (about +0.17 per unit), balancing the noise-seller flow against adverse selection.

Expected profit is linear in each trade, so my current short position does not change the per-side calculation.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 9.0}

**Posterior on red count R.** Draws are B, R, R, so the likelihood for R = r is proportional to (10−r)·r·(r−1). This gives R ∈ {2,…,9}, with mean 6.2 and SD about 1.83. So the public fair value is F = 6.2.

**Quote choice.** I'm risk-neutral, so the current short position of −1 doesn't change the per-side pricing, and each side can be priced separately (the ±3 limits don't bind here).

- **Ask:** Expected edge per quote is 0.65·P(v > A)·(A − 6.2) minus 0.35·E[(A − R)·1{R > A}]. Scanning values, the edge peaks near A ≈ 8.4 (about 0.234). A = 8.0 gives about 0.227, and A = 9.0 gives about 0.222.
- **Bid:** Expected edge per quote is 0.65·P(v < B)·(6.2 − B) minus 0.35·E[(B − R)·1{R < B}]. This peaks near B = 4.0 (about 0.218). B = 4.1 gives about 0.214, and B = 3.9 gives about 0.217.

The ask edge is slightly larger because the posterior is skewed toward higher values, so the informed sellers' threat is smaller on the bid side.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 8.4}

Quote 8 is the last quote, so I only need to price this one trade. My posterior on the red count (prior uniform, updated on the draws and the trade history) has a mean of about 8.1, with most mass on R = 9. Draw 1 was blue, so R ≤ 9.

- **Ask:** an informed buyer only arrives when R > ask, which is impossible for an ask at or above 9. Pricing against noise buyers alone, the best ask is about 1.8 above fair value, which is 9.9.
- **Bid:** an informed seller arrives when R < bid. Weighing that against noise sellers gives a best bid of about 6.0.

Both sides are independent for a single arrival, so I quote both.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 9.9}

info.raw:

Scoring a few candidate asks (A = 6, 7, 7.5, 8, 8.5, 9) gives net edges of about −0.10, +0.07, +0.10, +0.11, +0.10, +0.09, so the ask at 8.0 is best. By symmetry the bid at 2.0 has the same edge.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

Quote 1 traded at my bid of 2, so the seller had a valuation below 2. Under the rules, that trade history is public information. An informed seller only sells to me when R is 0 or 1, and a noise seller at fair value 5 is unlikely to value the contract below 2. Updating on this gives a posterior with P(R=0)=P(R=1)≈0.29 and P(R=2..10)≈0.047 each, so the public fair value is about 2.8.

Expected profit per quote, with the informed trader active 35% of the time and the noise trader 65%:
- **Bid:** the best bid is near 0. Its expected profit is about 0.22, which beats bids of 0.5 (about 0.20) or 1 (about 0.16). At 0 an informed seller (R≥0) never sells to me, and the noise traders with valuation below 0 are the only sellers.
- **Ask:** the best ask is near 6. Its expected profit is about 0.03, compared with about 0.025 at 5.5 and 0.019 at 6.5. Asks below about 5 lose money to informed buyers with R above the ask.

Quoting 0 bid and 6 ask.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 6.0}

**Fair value:** Before draw 1 the red count is uniform on 0..10, so the prior mean is 5. Conditioning on the trade history and the revealed red draw gives a posterior mean of about 8.1. Quote 1 (a seller at bid 2) pushes weight toward low R, while quote 2 (a buyer at ask 6) pushes weight toward high R. Draw 1 = red then pushes the mean up. The posterior puts about 89% of its mass on R ≥ 7, and R = 10 alone has about 26%.

**Quote choice:** The informed trader (35%) knows R. It sells to me at my bid only if R < bid, and buys at my ask only if R > ask. Noise traders (65%) have valuations around 8.1 with SD 2.4. Each side can be optimised separately:

- **Bid:** Maximising noise-trader profit minus informed adverse selection gives a peak near 6.0. At 6.0 the expected bid-side profit is about 0.177, and 5.9 and 6.1 are slightly worse.
- **Ask:** Posting at 10.0 means the informed buyer never trades, since R ≤ 10. Noise buyers still take it when their valuation exceeds 10, which is about a 22% chance, for an expected profit of about 0.27. Moving the ask lower loses more to informed buyers than it gains in noise flow.

I'm flat and the quote is within the 2.1 and 1.9 range around fair value, so I'll post a 6.0 bid and a 10.0 ask.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.0}

**Posterior after the public history:** Draw 1 = red makes the prior proportional to r. The quote 1 and 2 trades (sold at 2, bought at 6) and the quote 3 no-trade shift weight toward high R. My estimate is that the public fair value is about 8.3, with most mass on R = 7 to 10.

**Adverse selection:** An informed buyer hits my ask only if R > ask, and an informed seller hits my bid only if R < bid. Using the posterior, the expected profit per quote is roughly:
- Bid: about 0.21 at 6.2, with a noise-trader term that falls off as the bid rises and an informed-seller loss that grows.
- Ask: about 0.27 at 10.1, where the noise-buyer term peaks before the informed-buyer term matters.

Both sides are roughly flat near these levels, so I'm choosing bid 6.2 and ask 10.1. This is a one-quote myopic estimate and ignores inventory effects and the draw 2 reveal before stage 3.

{"bid": 6.2, "ask": 10.1}

**Quote 5: bid 6.0, ask 10.0**

- **Fair value:** After draws 1 and 2 are both red, the posterior on red count R is proportional to C(R,2), so E[R | two reds] = 8. Settlement value is R, so the public fair value is about 8.
- **Posterior:** Weights run from R=2 (about 0.6%) up to R=10 (about 27%), with mass concentrated at the top of the range.
- **Bid side:** Noise sellers arrive when their valuation is below the bid, and each such trade is worth about 8 − bid to us. Informed sellers arrive only when R is below the bid, costing us. Maximising the expected profit from this side gives a bid of roughly 5.7–6.0. The no-trade results at quotes 3 and 4 slightly downweight low R, which nudges the optimum up, so I chose 6.0.
- **Ask side:** Informed buyers only arrive when R is above the ask, and R cannot exceed 10. Quoting the ask at 10 means no informed trader can buy from us, and noise buyers still arrive often enough to make this the best ask.
- **Inventory:** Position is 0, so there's no skew needed.

This is an approximation: I didn't fully model how the earlier trade history changes the posterior.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.0}

**Posterior on red count N.** The prior is uniform, and draws 1 and 2 both came up red, so the weights are proportional to N(N-1). Folding in the trade history (a sale at bid 2, a purchase at ask 6, and no trades at 6/10 and 6.2/10.1 with a 6/10 quote in stage 3) gives a public fair value of about **8.74**. The posterior puts about 0.34 on N=10 and about 0.27 on N=9, with almost no mass below 6.

**Quote choice.** Informed traders can only buy from me above N=10 and only sell to me below N=6, so the adverse-selection cost is small.
- **Ask 10.5:** no informed trader can buy at this price (N ≤ 10), so only noise buyers trade. Their chance of valuing the contract above 10.5 is about 23%, which gives an expected profit of about +0.26 per quote.
- **Bid 6.9:** the informed sellers (N < 6.9) carry little posterior mass, so the cost is small. Noise sellers arrive about 22% of the time, which gives an expected profit of about +0.26.

Both sides are roughly equal in expected value, so I'm quoting both.

{"bid": 6.9, "ask": 10.5}

**Posterior on red count.** Three reds were drawn, so the posterior on R is proportional to C(R,3) for R = 3..10. Trade history shifts it upward: the sell at bid 2 was almost certainly noise, the buy at ask 6 favours R > 6, and four no-trades at bid 6 (informed sellers would have hit it for R < 6) favour R ≥ 7. My rough estimate puts the posterior mean near 9.0, with most mass on R = 7..10. The public fair value is roughly 8.9–9.0.

**Ask.** Informed buyers only buy when R > ask. Since R ≤ 10, an ask at 10 or above carries no informed risk. Against noise buyers (valuation about N(8.95, 2.4)), the expected profit per unit, P(V > a) × (a − 8.95), peaks near a ≈ 10.7.

**Bid.** Informed sellers hit the bid when R < bid. Bidding 7.0 avoids the large R = 7 mass, since an informed seller at R = 7 would only trade at a bid above 7. Noise sellers at 7.0 still give a positive expected profit of about 1.95 per unit. Raising the bid above 7 costs more in informed adverse selection than it gains in noise flow.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 10.7}

**Posterior on red count R:** The first three draws were all red, so the likelihood of the data given R is C(R,3). With a uniform prior, the posterior is proportional to C(R,3) for R = 3..10. The posterior mean is E[R] = 8.6, which is the public fair value for noise traders.

**Ask:** An informed buyer arrives only when R > ask. Above 10, no buyer can be informed, so the ask only faces noise traders. Selling profit per noise trade is (ask − 8.6) × P(valuation > ask), which peaks around 10.35. Rounding up to a tick gives **10.4**, with expected value about +0.27 per unit.

**Bid:** An informed seller arrives only when R < bid. Balancing adverse selection against the noise-trader gain, expected profit peaks near a bid of 6.4 at about +0.22 per unit.

Only one counterparty arrives, so both sides can be quoted. This is the last quote, so inventory after it does not matter.

game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** Before any draws are revealed, R is uniform on 0–10, so the prior mean is 5. Quote 1 was already at this optimum, so I'll keep it.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 100}

Posterior: two blue draws give weights C(11-r, 2) on R = 0..9, so the public fair value is 10 × E[R] = 10 × 2.25 = **22.5**.

The informed side is the main risk. Informed buyers take the ask only when the settlement exceeds it, and informed sellers hit the bid only when the settlement is below it. Noise traders are centred on 22.5 with sd 35. Weighting each side by the 0.5 probability of each counterparty type, I get roughly:

- **Ask:** the expected profit peaks around 55–60 (about 2.3 per quote). Near 35 it falls to roughly zero, because informed buyers pick off the high-settlement states.
- **Bid:** informed sellers only hit a bid above 0 when R = 0 or 1. A bid of 0 is close to optimal (about 2.9 per quote) and avoids negative prices.

This is a one-shot estimate and ignores the later reveals, so I'm keeping the quote wide.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 60}

**Bid:** Informed sellers only hit a bid when 10R is below it, and R = 0 is the only state that puts 10R below the low bids I'd consider. Noise sellers arrive when their valuation (about N(26.4, 35)) is below the bid. Expected profit per bid level is maximized near 0, and bidding 0 avoids informed sales entirely. Bid = 0.

**Ask:** Informed buyers take the ask when 10R is above it, which mostly means R ≥ 7 (about 2% probability). Noise buyers arrive when their valuation exceeds the ask. Expected profit is maximized near 60, where informed adverse selection is small and the noise-buyer tail is still meaningful. Ask = 60.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 60}

Posterior after draws 1–3 are blue and the quote 3–4 history (including the buy at 60): P(R) ≈ 0.09, 0.32, 0.23, 0.15, 0.09, 0.05, 0.03, 0.03, 0.01 for R = 0..8. That gives E[R] ≈ 2.3, so the public fair value is about 23.

- **Bid 0:** No informed seller can arrive, since V ≥ 0. Only noise sellers with valuation below 0 (about 25%) would trade, for an expected edge of roughly 2.9.
- **Ask 55:** Informed buyers arrive only when V > 55 (R ≥ 6), and the noise buyer probability is about 18%. This maximizes expected edge at about 2.5, slightly above ask 60 and ask 50.


{"bid": 0, "ask": 55}

Blue draws 1-3 shift the posterior on red count R toward low values, so the public fair value is 10 × E[R] = 10 × 1.6 = 16.

- **Ask:** Expected profit from an ask at 50 is about +2.6. Informed buyers only take it when R ≥ 6, and noise buyers take it with probability about 0.17. Nearby asks (45, 48, 52, 55) are slightly worse.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 50}

Posterior on red count after the revealed blues and the trade history: R=0 is downweighted because the informed trader would have sold to us at bid 10 on quotes 1-2, and it didn't. Posterior mean V ≈ 17. Noise valuations centre near 17 with SD 35.

- **Bid 0:** An informed seller only hits a bid when V < bid, and V ≥ 0, so bidding 0 avoids adverse selection. Noise sellers still arrive, and we profit from buying below the mean.
- **Ask 45:** Informed buyers take the ask only when V > 45, which is rare under this posterior. Noise buyers at 45 pay well above the mean. The expected edge peaks around 45, and asks near 25 or below lose money.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 45}

**Fair value:** Conditioning on the four blue draws, the posterior on red balls is proportional to C(11−R, 4) for R = 0..7. That gives E[R] = 7/6, so the public fair value is about 11.67.

**Ask:** Informed buyers take the ask when 10R > A. Noise buyers take it when their valuation (mean 11.67, sd 35) exceeds A. Summing expected profit (A − V) over both arrivals, the best ask is about 40 (expected profit ≈ 2.8). Below about 20 the informed buyers make the ask a loss. Above about 50, too few noise buyers arrive.

**Bid:** Informed sellers only arrive when 10R < B, which is essentially never for B ≤ 0. The noise-seller term 0.5·P(N < B)·(11.67 − B) is maximised near B ≈ −14.6, so I'd round to −15. That is a negative price, which the rules don't forbid but which is unusual. If negative bids are rejected, the step is simply unreadable or ignored, so the risk is small. A bid of 0 would be the conservative choice, with expected value about 2.2 versus 3.0.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 9.0}

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 9.4}

Two draws were red, so the posterior on red count R is proportional to R(R-1). Taking the sale as evidence about N and weighting informed and noise traders, the posterior mean is about 2.8. I'm long one unit, so I'll skew slightly toward selling by lowering both sides a little.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 3.5}

Under the stated model, the two earlier sells at our bid are evidence that R is low. Bayes-updating on them (with noise-trader valuations centred on the prior mean of 5 for the first trade and the updated fair value for the second) gives a public fair value of about 1.7, with most posterior mass on R = 0 or 1.

Expected edge per side, given fair value ≈ 1.7:
- **Bid:** buying at 0 earns about +0.26, mostly from noise sellers whose valuation falls below 0. No informed trader has R < 0, so there is no adverse selection at that price. Higher bids are worse, since informed sellers with R = 0 or 1 start to bite.
- **Ask:** selling at 4 earns about +0.08, near the best of the grid I checked. Lower asks give less edge, and higher asks lose noise-buyer flow.

Position is +2, but the objective is risk-neutral expected profit at settlement, so inventory alone doesn't justify a quote.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 4.0}

**Reasoning**

- **Public fair value.** Draw 1 = blue gives a posterior on red count proportional to (10 − R), with mean 3. The earlier trades carry information through informed traders, who sell to us only when R is below our bid. Updating on the two sells at our bid and the no-trade at quote 3 brings the fair value down to about 1.2.
- **Bid.** Informed sellers arrive only when R < bid, so a bid at 0 faces no informed flow. Noise sellers arrive when their valuation, around 1.2 ± 2.4, is below the bid. A bid of 0 is the best non-negative bid for expected profit. A slightly negative bid would be marginally better, but I'm not confident negative prices are accepted.
- **Ask.** Selling to noise buyers is profitable above fair value. Informed buyers take the ask when R exceeds it, and that cost rises with the ask. Balancing the two gives an optimum near 2.6.
- **Inventory.** Since the objective is expected settlement profit, the +2 position doesn't change the myopic quote. It only matters for the ±5 limits, which are not close.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 2.6}

Posterior fair value: with draw 1 = 0, the posterior on red count is proportional to (10−n), giving E[N] = 3. Draw 2 and draw 3 aren't revealed yet, and the trade history is only weakly informative, so I keep fair value at about 3.

Expected profit per quote, with 35% informed traders and noise traders centred on 3 with sd 2.4:
- **Ask:** profit is roughly flat at 0.146 for asks between 5.5 and 5.8. I'll use 5.5.
- **Bid:** profit peaks near 0.5 (about 0.21). Being long +1 also argues for keeping the bid low.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 5.5}

**Posterior:** R is uniform on 0..10, and draw 1 = blue gives a posterior proportional to (10 − r). That puts the prior mean at 3. The trade history pulls it down: the two early sells at our bids (2 and 1.9) and the buy at 2.6 are only partly offset by the no-trade quotes, so my rough Bayesian update gives a fair value of about 1.7 to 2.5. I'll take about 2 as the central estimate.

**Bid:** Expected profit from buying at B is roughly 0.65·Φ((B−μ)/2.4)·(μ−B) minus 0.35·E[(B−V)⁺] for informed sellers. This is maximised near B = 0, since adverse selection from informed sellers grows quickly above that.

**Ask:** Expected profit from selling at A is roughly 0.65·(1−Φ((A−μ)/2.4))·(A−μ) minus 0.35·E[(V−A)⁺]. This peaks around A ≈ 4 for μ ≈ 1.7 and around 4.5 for μ ≈ 2.5, so 4.0 is a reasonable compromise.

The spread is wide because the noise-trader standard deviation (2.4) is large relative to the uncertainty about the value.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4.0}

Posterior after two blue draws: the weights on R are proportional to (10−R)(9−R), which gives E[R] = 2.0 exactly. The fair value is about 2.0.

- **Bid:** Informed sellers hit a bid only when R is below it, so with R ≥ 0 a bid near 1.7 loses money on net. A bid of 0 earns roughly +0.26 per quote in expectation from noise sellers alone, and I'm already long, so I don't want to add much.
- **Ask:** Expected edge peaks around 4.0–4.3 (about +0.19 per quote), balancing noise buyers against informed buyers who lift an ask when R is high.

I'll quote bid 0 and ask 4.2.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4.2}

**Posterior after two blue draws:** The likelihood of two blues given R = r is proportional to (10−r)(9−r), so the posterior weights on r = 0..8 are proportional to 90, 72, 56, 42, 30, 20, 12, 6, 2. This gives a fair value of E[R] = 2.0, with standard deviation about 1.9.

**Bid:** Informed sellers only hit a bid when R < bid. At a bid of 0 they can never do so profitably, because R ≥ 0, so there is no adverse selection. Raising the bid above 0 adds about 0.35 × P(R=0) ≈ 0.095 of adverse-selection loss per unit, against only about 0.02 of extra noise-trader gain. So bid 0.

**Ask:** Expected profit per quote, as a function of the ask a, is 0.35·E[(a−R)·1{R>a}] + 0.65·P(noise buys)·(a−2). At a = 2 this is about −0.27, so the ask must sit well above the fair value. The profit peaks around a ≈ 4.1–4.2 (about 0.19). Since I'm slightly long (+1), I'll take the lower end of that flat region to encourage a sale.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4.1}

**Fair value.** Two blue draws and the trade history put the posterior on red balls R at about 0 (34%) and 1 (52%), with a long thin tail. The public fair value is about 0.98. The informed-trader risk is mostly on the ask side: an informed buyer appears only if R > ask, and that is rare (about 7% for R ≥ 3).

**Ask.** Noise buyers arrive at ask A with probability P(V > A), where V ~ N(0.98, 2.4²). Expected profit is maximised near A = 3.0, with an expected value of about 0.24 per quote.

**Bid.** Informed sellers only arrive when R < B. Since R ≥ 0, a bid at or below 0 faces no informed risk, so only noise sellers matter. Expected profit is maximised near B = -0.8 to -0.9, about 0.265 per quote. A bid of 0 would earn only about 0.22, because informed sellers appear whenever R = 0.

This quote assumes negative prices are accepted. The bid is well below the fair value because it captures the noise-seller flow with no informed risk.

{"bid": -0.8, "ask": 3.0}

**Fair value.** Three blue draws leave the urn with R red balls among the 7 undrawn balls. The posterior on R is proportional to C(10−R, 3), which gives P(R=0..7) ≈ 0.364, 0.255, 0.170, 0.106, 0.061, 0.030, 0.012, 0.003. Its mean is exactly 1.4, so the public fair value is 1.4.

**Bid.** An informed seller can only hit a bid below R ≥ 0, so a bid of −0.4 faces no informed flow. The noise trader sells to me at −0.4 with probability ≈ 0.23, earning about 1.8 per unit against fair value. Expected contribution ≈ +0.26.

**Ask.** Informed buyers arrive when R > a, which is adverse. Balancing that against the noise buyer's probability and margin, the expected contribution peaks near a ≈ 3.5–3.6 at about +0.22. I'll use 3.6.

Both sides are positive in expectation, and the bid carries no adverse selection.

{"bid": -0.4, "ask": 3.6}

**Reasoning (quote 11, short 1 unit, 2 quotes left)**

Three blue draws give a posterior on red count proportional to C(10−r, 3), which is zero for r ≥ 8. The trade history also carries information, since informed buyers at asks 2.6, 3.0 and 3.6 imply R above those levels, while the sells at bids 2 and 1.9 imply R of 1 or less. Combining these, my approximate posterior is:

- R = 0: ~26%
- R = 1: ~35%
- R = 4: ~32%
- Everything else: ~7%
- Mean ≈ 1.8

The posterior is bimodal, so the quotes should sit at the edges of the clusters:

- **Bid 0:** Buying at 0 is worth about 1.85 per unit in expectation against noise sellers. Informed sellers only sell when R < bid, and nothing is below 0, so this avoids adverse selection. Raising the bid above 0 starts to attract informed sales from R = 0, which costs more than it gains.
- **Ask 4:** Selling at 4 is worth about 2.15 per unit against noise buyers. Informed buyers only buy when R > ask, and R = 4 is not above 4, so the ~32% mass at R = 4 is excluded. Asking 4.1 or higher gives up a little and asking below 4 lets informed buyers take the R = 4 mass.

This is a myopic optimisation, and the posterior is approximate.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4}

**Reasoning for quote 12 (final quote)**

- **Posterior on red count:** Three blue draws imply a posterior proportional to C(10−R, 3). The trade history also matters. The early sells at 2 and 1.9 point to low R, while the later buys at 3 and 3.6 point to higher R. Combining these roughly gives a public fair value of about 1.6, with a lot of mass on R = 0, 1 and a meaningful chunk on R = 4.
- **Bid side:** Informed sellers only trade when R < bid. Since R ≥ 0, a bid of 0 gives them no informed trades. Any noise seller that hits 0 pays at most our valuation, so the trade is non-negative for us in expectation.
- **Ask side:** An informed buyer takes the ask only when R > ask. An ask of exactly 4 excludes R = 4, which carries substantial posterior weight, and leaves only R ≥ 5 (small mass) as informed buyers. Pricing below 4 would invite informed buys from R = 4. Pricing above 4 loses noise-trader fills faster than it gains edge.

Expected edge from this quote is roughly +0.25 on each side under this model. Both prices are sensible, though the exact fair value is approximate.

Given the two blue draws, the posterior over red balls is proportional to (10−R)(9−R), so E[R] = 2 and the public fair value is 20.

Each quote is hit by at most one counterparty, so expected profit per quote is the sum of the two sides. The informed traders (prob 0.2) only trade against us when they know the settlement is on the wrong side of our price. Noise traders (prob 0.8) trade when their valuation, centred on 20 with sd 47, is past our quote.

- **Ask 58:** Noise buyers come in with probability about 0.21 and earn us about 38 each. The informed buyers, who appear when R ≥ 6, cost about 0.09 in expectation. Net is roughly +6.3. Asks of 57 and 58 are nearly equal, and 58 is marginally better.
- **Bid −15:** Noise sellers come in with probability about 0.23 and earn us about 35 each. No informed seller appears, since 10R < −15 is impossible. Net is roughly +6.4, the best integer bid.

The rules don't forbid a negative bid, so I'm quoting the expected-profit-maximising pair even though it looks unusual.

{"bid": -15, "ask": 58}

**Posterior:** Draws 1 and 2 were both blue, so the posterior on red count R is proportional to (10−R)(9−R). This gives E[R] = 2, so the public fair value is 10 × 2 = **20**.

**Bid:** Informed sellers only sell to me when 10R < bid. Bids at or below 0 therefore attract no informed sellers, so only noise traders trade. Maximising (20 − B) × 0.8 × Φ((B − 20)/47) gives an optimum near B ≈ −15.

**Ask:** Noise buyers come in at rate 0.8 × (1 − Φ((A − 20)/47)), and informed buyers come in when 10R > A. Including the informed buyers' adverse selection, expected profit peaks around A ≈ 56–58. A = 57 is the best integer.

{"bid": -15, "ask": 57}

**Quote 5 reasoning**

- **Posterior on red count:** The draws 0, 0, 1 give a posterior proportional to R(10−R)(9−R) for R = 0..10, which peaks around R = 3–4. The posterior mean is about 3.80 red balls.
- **Fair value:** 10 × 3.80 ≈ 38.0.
- **Adverse selection:** The 20% informed traders buy from me only when 10R > ask and sell to me only when 10R < bid. Noise traders trade roughly symmetrically around 38 with standard deviation 47.
- **Breakeven prices:** Conditional on a customer buying at ask a, the expected settlement value is about 41.3 for asks near 41–42, so the ask must be at least 42 to avoid losing money on the trade. Conditional on a customer selling to me at bid b, the expected settlement value is about 34.8, so the bid can be at most 34.
- **Inventory:** I'm short 1, which mildly favours a slightly higher bid to buy back, but 35 would lose money on average, so I keep the bid at 34.

{"bid": 34, "ask": 42}

**Fair value:** The first three draws (0, 0, 1) give a posterior on red balls R with mean about 3.8, so the value 10R has a mean of about 38. The trade history (buys at 57 and 42) is informative about R through the informed traders, which pushes the fair value to roughly 42. I used 42 as the centre.

**Ask:** Selling at ask *a* earns about 0.8·P(noise buys)·(a − 42) minus the informed-buyer adverse selection, which is small here. With noise sd 47, this peaks near a ≈ 78–80. I'm at −2, so one more sale is allowed (to −3).

**Bid:** Buying at bid *b* peaks near 7–8, since informed sellers are essentially absent (no posterior mass below R = 1). I'm short, so buying back is allowed.

Both sides are roughly flat near their optima, so the expected edge is about 6.3 per quote on each side.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 78}

Posting a low bid to buy back part of the short, with the ask pulled as required.

- **Fair value:** Draws 1 to 4 (0, 0, 1, 0) imply a posterior on red balls of about 3 before the trade history. Folding in the trades at quotes 1 to 6 (the buys at 57, 42, and 78 suggest buyers with high valuations) moves the posterior mean to about 3.4 red balls, a public value near 34.
- **Expected profit from a bid b:** Noise sellers arrive when their valuation, about 34 plus N(0, 47), falls below b, and each such trade earns about 34 - b. Informed sellers only arrive when 10R < b, which is impossible for b ≤ 0 under this posterior.
- **Optimum:** Expected profit peaks near b = -1 to -2 (about 6.4). Those bids are close to equal in value, so I take -2.

game.description: An urn holds 9 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 9. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.

info.raw:
Before any draws are revealed, the public fair value is the prior mean of 4.5. The informed counterparty knows the exact red count, so quoting near 4.5 loses money on the informed flow. Each side's expected profit is roughly the noise-trader edge minus the expected loss to informed buyers or sellers, and the best trade-off is at the extremes of the support. An ask of 9 is almost never hit by an informed trader (only if R = 9 is it even worth buying, and then only at zero profit). A bid of 0 is similarly safe, and the noise traders still provide edge on both sides.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 9}

At quote 3 nothing is revealed and there are no trades, so the public fair value is E[R] = 4.5. The contract is worth between 0 and 9, so an informed counterparty can never profitably trade against a bid of 0 or an ask of 9. Any trade at those prices comes from a noise trader.

With a noise trader valuation of about N(4.5, 4.3):
- Ask 9: P(noise buys) ≈ 0.148, profit per trade ≈ 4.5, so expected contribution ≈ 0.5 × 0.148 × 4.5 ≈ 0.33.
- Bid 0: P(noise sells) ≈ 0.148, profit per trade ≈ 4.5, so expected contribution ≈ 0.33.

Tighter quotes such as an ask of 7 or a bid of 2 add informed-trader losses that outweigh the extra noise volume. Quoting 0/9 keeps adverse selection at zero this quote, and it matches the earlier quotes.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 9}

**Posterior after draw 1 = blue:** P(R = r) ∝ (9 − r), so P(r) = (9 − r)/45 for r = 0..9. This gives fair value F = 120/45 ≈ 2.67, with standard deviation ≈ 2.2.

**Ask side:** Informed buyers take the ask only when R > a, costing me a − R. Noise buyers take it with probability P(N(F, 4.3) > a), earning a − F on average. Maximising 0.5·[Σ_{r>a} P(r)(a − r)] + 0.5·P(V > a)·(a − F) gives a profit of about 0.33 at a ≈ 6.5–6.8. Since R rarely exceeds 7, adverse selection is small, and the wide noise-trader distribution makes high asks profitable. The previous ask of 3.9 was roughly break-even.

**Bid side:** Informed sellers hit the bid only when R < b. For b = 0 there is no informed risk, and noise sellers arrive with probability P(V < 0) ≈ 0.27 at an expected gain of F − 0 ≈ 2.67. Profit is about 0.36, slightly better than b = 0.5 (about 0.28). Negative bids would be marginally better in the model, but I'll stay at 0 to avoid relying on negative prices being valid.

Quote: bid 0, ask 6.7.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 6.7}

**Posterior after the reveals and no-trade history**

- Prior on red count R is uniform on 0..9. Draw 1 = blue gives weight (9−R), so E[R | draw 1 = 0] = 8/3 ≈ 2.67.
- No trade at quotes 4 and 5 is evidence. A no-trade means an informed counterparty would not have traded, so R lay inside the quoted band. Quote 4 (band [1.6, 3.9]) favours R = 2, 3. Quote 5 (band [0, 6.7]) favours R ≤ 6. Updating on both gives a fair value of about 2.46, with most mass on R = 2 and 3.

**Quote 6**

- Ask: expected profit is 0.5·Σ_{R>A} p(R)(A−R) + 0.5·Φ((FV−A)/4.3)·(A−FV). This is maximised near A ≈ 6.0 (≈ +0.36). Higher asks lose noise-trader volume, and lower asks give away too much to informed buyers.
- Bid: informed sellers only appear for R < B, which has essentially no mass at B ≤ 0. The noise-only optimum is slightly negative (about −0.8, worth roughly +0.02 more than B = 0). I'm quoting 0 to stay within ordinary price levels, since that small gain isn't worth the risk of a rejected negative price.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 6.0}

Under the stated model, the public fair value is E[R | two blue draws] = 1.75, since the posterior weight on R is proportional to (9-R)(8-R). Maximising expected settlement profit on each side gives:

- **Ask:** the first-order condition (a-1.75)·φ(a) = P(noise buys) + P(informed buys) has its root near a ≈ 5.35, so I round up to **5.4**.
- **Bid:** the informed seller needs R < b, and R ≥ 0, so informed sellers never trade at b ≤ 0. The optimum is then set by noise sellers alone, which gives b ≈ -1.5. The rules don't impose a non-negative price floor, so I quote it, though it is unusual and the gain over a bid of 0 is small (about 0.07).


{"bid": -1.5, "ask": 5.4}

**Reasoning**

- **Posterior on red count.** With draws 1 and 2 both blue, the weight on N is proportional to (9−N)(8−N), which gives a mean of 1.75 before any trading information.
- **Trading history.** The buy at 5.4 suggests a counterparty valued above 5.4. That is much more likely from an informed trader holding N ≥ 6 or from a noise trader, which shifts the mean up. The no-trade at quote 4 (bid 1.6, ask 3.9) pulls mass toward N = 2 or 3. Combining these, I estimate the mean at about 2.3, with standard deviation about 1.4.
- **Ask side.** Noise traders have valuations centred near 2.3 with standard deviation 4.3. Informed buyers only appear when N > ask, and the posterior mass above 6 is small. Expected profit from selling at ask a peaks near 6.0.
- **Bid side.** Expected profit from buying at bid b peaks slightly below zero, around −0.5 to −0.8, because noise sellers arrive when their valuation falls below b. I chose −0.5, which is nearly as good and more robust if the public fair value is a bit higher than my estimate.

{"bid": -0.5, "ask": 6.0}

**Posterior on R.** Both revealed draws were blue, so the likelihood of the draws is proportional to (9−R)(8−R). The trade history also matters:
- Quote 4 (bid 1.6, ask 3.9) did not trade. Informed traders would have traded for R ≤ 1 or R ≥ 4, so this favours R = 2 or 3.
- Quotes 5, 6 and 8 did not trade. Informed traders would have bought for R ≥ 7, so this shrinks the high-R tail.
- Quote 7 was a buy at 5.4. Informed traders buy only for R ≥ 6, so this shifts weight up to R ≥ 6.

Combining these gives an approximate posterior with mean E[R] ≈ 2.3, and roughly P(R=2) ≈ 0.40, P(R=3) ≈ 0.28, P(R=6) ≈ 0.05, P(R≥7) ≈ 0.001. These are approximations, since I ignored second-order effects of the trade history on the noise traders' valuations.

**Final quote.** Nothing trades after this quote, so each side is evaluated on its own.
- **Ask:** a sale at ask a moves the position from −1 to −2 and is worth a − R. The noise-buyer term is about 0.5·P(v > a)·(a − 2.3), and the informed term is only negative for R > a. The expected value peaks at a ≈ 6.0 (≈ 0.36), where the informed term is negligible.
- **Bid:** a purchase at bid b is worth R − b. Informed sellers exist only for R < b, so for b ≤ 0 only noise sellers matter. The expected value 0.5·P(v < b)·(2.3 − b) peaks near b ≈ −0.9 (≈ 0.37).

{"bid": -0.9, "ask": 6.0}

game.description: An urn holds 8 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 8. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.

info.raw:
With no information yet, the public fair value is 10 × E[R] = 10 × 4 = 40. Each side is independent in expected profit, so I optimise the ask and bid separately.

- **Ask side:** A noise buyer trades if its valuation exceeds the ask. My expected gain from that trade is (ask − 40). An informed buyer trades only if 10R > ask, and it costs me (10R − ask) per trade. The sum over both is largest near an ask of 80, where no informed buyer can trade (10R ≤ 80) and the noise-trader gain is still about 0.35 per quote.
- **Bid side:** By symmetry, the same logic gives a bid of 0.

Quoting 80 and 0 is roughly a myopic best. It is also a wide market, so it trades rarely and keeps inventory at zero until the revealed draws add information.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 80}

Fair value after draw 1 = blue: the posterior on red balls R is proportional to (8 − R), so E[R] = 84/36 ≈ 2.33 and the fair value is about 23.3.

- **Bid:** Informed sellers only hit a bid of 0 if V < 0, which never happens. Noise sellers at 0 still trade about 11% of the time, each at an expected edge of about 23. Raising the bid to 1 or more lets informed holders of V = 0 sell to me, which costs more than the extra noise flow gains. Best integer bid: 0.
- **Ask:** Informed buyers take the ask whenever V exceeds it. Among integer asks, 50 gives the best trade-off. Asks of 49 and 51 both score lower.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 50}

**Posterior after draw 1 = blue:** P(R = r) ∝ (8 − r), so E[R] = 7/3 and the naive value is about 23.3.

**Update from the no-trade history:** A no-trade at a quote with bid b and ask a rules out informed counterparties whose value 10R lies outside [b, a]. Quotes 2–3 (bid 10, ask 70) rule out R = 0 and R = 8. Quotes 4–5 (bids 0 and 9, asks 50) rule out R = 6–8, and quote 5 also rules out R = 0. Reweighting gives roughly:

| R | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 0.03 | 0.27 | 0.23 | 0.19 | 0.15 | 0.11 | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0 |

The public fair value is about 10 × 2.61 ≈ 26.

**Quote choice:** Each side's expected profit is the informed-trader loss plus the noise-trader gain, and the two sides add because only one counterparty arrives.
- Ask: the informed buyers (R ≥ 5) are small in probability, while noise buyers (valuation ≈ 26 ± 19) make a higher ask profitable. Expected profit peaks near 50 (about 1.10 per quote, versus about 1.09 at 49 and 1.09 at 48).
- Bid: informed sellers only come from R = 0 once the bid is 10. Expected profit peaks near 10 (about 1.46, versus about 1.45 at 9 and 1.33 at 11).

The spread is wide and skewed because the posterior mass sits low, but the ask is set high enough that the noise-trader gain outweighs the informed-trader loss. This is a one-step myopic estimate and ignores what later trades will reveal.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 50}

**Posterior on red balls.** The prior is uniform on R = 0..8. Two blue draws give likelihood (8−R)(7−R), which gives weights 56, 42, 30, 20, 12, 6, 2, 0, 0 for R = 0..8.

**Inference from no trades.** Informed counterparties would have traded whenever 10R fell outside the bid/ask band. Their absence down-weights R values that would have triggered a trade. The main effects are:
- R = 0 is excluded by the bids at 9–10 (quotes 2, 3, 5, 6).
- R ≥ 6 is excluded by the asks at 50 (quotes 4–6).
- R = 8 is also excluded by the ask at 70 (quotes 2, 3).

Roughly, each violated quote halves the weight. This gives posterior probabilities of about R=0: 0.03, R=1: 0.37, R=2: 0.26, R=3: 0.18, R=4: 0.11, R=5: 0.05, R=6: 0.002. The posterior mean of R is about 2.12, so the public fair value is about 21.

**Optimal quotes (one-period expected profit).**
- Ask: a sale at ask a loses to informed buyers when 10R > a and gains from noise buyers whose valuation (fair 21, sd 19) exceeds a. Expected profit peaks near a = 40 (about 1.23, versus 1.21 at 41 and 1.19 at 39).
- Bid: a purchase at bid b loses to informed sellers when 10R < b and gains from noise sellers whose valuation falls below b. Expected profit is flat around b = 5–6 (about 1.52).

The two sides are separable because only one counterparty arrives per quote. These are myopic one-quote optima and ignore the later quotes, so they are approximate given the modelling simplifications (for example, noise no-trade probabilities are treated as roughly constant).

{"bid": 6, "ask": 40}

**Reasoning (brief):**

- **Draws:** Two blues were revealed, so the posterior on red count R favours low R. The prior fair value was 15 before the draws; two blues alone give 15 and a quote-7 sell at bid 6 pushes it lower.
- **Quote 7:** The sell at bid 6 is much more likely if R = 0, since an informed seller sells only when 10R < 6. Taking that trade into account, the public fair value is roughly 7 if only trades are conditioned on, or roughly 20 if non-trades in earlier quotes are also conditioned on. I don't know which the game uses, so I weighed both.
- **Bid:** Bid 0 is robust. An informed seller never sells at 0, and noise sellers still hit it at positive expected profit. Higher bids pick up informed sells from R = 0 and do worse under both models.
- **Ask:** I am long 1, so I want to sell. Asks around 40 maximise the average expected profit across the two models. The trade-only model peaks near 29–30, but 40 is only slightly worse there and much better under the other model. Informed buyers appear only above roughly 40, which limits adverse selection.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 40}

**Posterior:** Two blue draws mean the urn holds R red balls with weight (8−R)(7−R), for R = 0..6. This gives E[R] = 1.5, so the public fair value is 10 × 1.5 = **15**.

**Bid side:** Buying at bid b earns 15 − b against noise sellers, with probability Φ((b − 15)/19). Informed sellers only sell when 10R < b, and at b = 0 none do. The value is about 3.22 at b = 0, and every higher integer bid does worse, so I'll use **bid = 0**.

info.raw:
Before any reveals, the public fair value is E[10R] = 10 × 11 × 0.3 = 33. Informed counterparties trade on the true value, so I need a wide enough spread to cover adverse selection. I checked symmetric quotes around 33 by computing expected profit from informed and noise flow. Tight quotes (30/36) lose money, and the expected profit peaks near a 46 ask and 20 bid, which is about 0.9 per quote.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 46}

Fair value is 10 × E[R] = 10 × 11 × 0.3 = 33, since nothing has been revealed yet. Noise traders are uninformative about R, so they only bring expected profit of (A − 33) on a buy at ask A or (33 − B) on a sell at bid B. Informed traders hit us only when the true value is on the wrong side of our price, which costs us.

Working through the binomial distribution of R (mean 3.3) and trading off the informed-trader losses against the noise-trader gains:
- The ask at 46 maximises expected profit on that side (about +0.34), with informed buys costing about −0.66 and noise buys earning about +1.00.
- The bid at 20 maximises expected profit on that side (about +0.54). Just above 20, the informed-sell losses jump when R = 2 becomes a sell at a bid of 21 or more.

Both prices match quote 1, and I'm flat, so I'll keep them.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 46}

I'm keeping the same quotes as the last two steps. With nothing revealed, the public fair value is 11 × 0.3 × 10 = 33. Against the 35% informed flow, I checked expected profit per side: the bid is near its best at about 20 (net about +0.54), and the ask is near its best at about 46 (net about +0.34). Both are positive and close to the maximum.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 46}

Quote 6: bid 20, ask 43.

Draws 1 and 2 give the 9 unknown balls an independent 0.3 red chance each, so the prior is 10K = 10 + 10·Bin(9, 0.3). The quote-4 sale at 25 implies an informed seller with value below 25, so K ≤ 2. The quote-5 no-trade slightly disfavours K ∈ {3,4,5}. After updating on both, the posterior mean settlement is about 31.3, which is the public fair value.

- **Bid:** the best bid is about 20. Above 20, an informed seller with K = 2 (value 20) starts selling to us at a loss, and the gain from noise sellers doesn't offset it.
- **Ask:** around 43. The informed buyers (K ≥ 5) and the noise-buyer edge balance near that level.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 43}

**Quote 7: bid 30, ask 57**

Draws 1 and 3 were red and draw 2 was blue, so two reds are known. The 8 unseen balls are independent with red probability 0.3, so the settlement value is V = 20 + 10K with K ~ Binomial(8, 0.3). That gives a public fair value of 44.

Each side's expected edge is its spread against the fair value, minus losses to informed traders (35%) who only trade when V is on the wrong side of our price. Noise traders are independent of V, so they cost us nothing beyond the spread.

- **Ask:** the edge peaks around 55–58. At 57 it is about +0.55, versus about −1.9 at 44.
- **Bid:** the edge peaks around 30, at about +0.72. It is negative at 40 because V = 20 and 30 are relatively likely.

Position +1 does not change the expected-profit calculation, since inventory is marked at fair value. Both sides stay open.

{"bid": 30, "ask": 57}

**Fair value:** The painting is iid Bernoulli(0.3) per ball, so the unseen balls stay iid given the observed draws. Two of the three revealed draws are red, leaving 8 unseen balls, so E[red] = 2 + 8×0.3 = 4.4 and the public fair value is 44.

**Informed-trader distribution:** Settlement V = 10×(2 + Bin(8, 0.3)), so V takes values 20, 30, …, 100 with probabilities roughly 0.06, 0.20, 0.30, 0.25, 0.14, 0.05, 0.01 for 20 through 80.

**Expected edge per side:** Each arriving counterparty is informed with probability 0.35 (trades only when V is beyond our quote) or noise with probability 0.65 (valuation ~ N(44, 11), trades when beyond our quote). The two sides are separable because only one counterparty arrives.

- Ask side: the expected profit per quote, a ≈ 56 gives the highest value (≈0.55), with 55 and 57 close behind.
- Bid side: b = 30 gives the highest value (≈0.72). At b = 31 the informed sellers at V = 30 start trading, which lowers the value.

Being long 1 doesn't change the expected value in a risk-neutral objective, but lowering the ask slightly, as 56 does, also encourages buyers to take the unit off us.

{"bid": 30, "ask": 56}

**Quote 9: bid 20, ask 45**

The public fair value is about 34, well below the naive 44 from the three revealed draws. The two sales to us at 25 and 30 and the earlier no-trades are informative under the rules, and I've updated for them. The posterior on the settlement value V is roughly 20 (25%), 30 (25%), 40 (37%), 50 (11%), with the remainder above 50.

- **Ask at 45:** The informed buyer only takes it if V ≥ 50, and noise buyers at 45 are priced at about 34 in expectation. Expected profit on this side is about +0.80. Asks of 44 and 46 score about the same.
- **Bid at 20:** Informed sellers only hit it if V < 20, and the lowest possible value is 20, so they never trade here. Noise sellers at 20 leave a large edge against the 34 fair value. Expected profit on this side is about +0.91, and higher bids score worse.

Both sides are priced to maximise expected profit at settlement. I haven't modelled the position limits or later quotes beyond this step.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 45}

**Reasoning**

- Draws 1 to 4 show 3 reds, so the red count is R = 3 + X, where X ~ Bin(7, 0.3). The prior mean is R = 5.1, or 51 in settlement value.
- The no-trade history is informative. An informed counterparty trades whenever V falls outside our spread, so the non-trades at quotes 1 to 10 favour values inside those spreads. Updating on that, the posterior is roughly V=30: 12%, V=40: 79%, V=50: 7%, V≥60: 2%. The public fair value is about 40.
- Bid side: the value of a bid b is 0.65·Φ((b−40)/11)·(40−b), minus informed losses for any V below b. Informed sellers need V<b, so a bid of 30 avoids them entirely (V=30 is not strictly below 30). This is roughly the best bid.
- Ask side: an ask of about 49 to 50 is near-optimal. Noise buyers at 50 pay roughly 10 above fair value, and the only informed buyers left are at V≥60, which has about 2% probability.

Quote 11 is bid 30, ask 50.

{"bid": 30, "ask": 50}

The posterior has the 7 unseen balls still independent with red probability 0.3, so expected reds = 3 + 7(0.3) = 5.1 and the public fair value is 51. Informed counterparties trade only when they see a profitable edge, so each side's expected profit is a noise-trader term minus an adverse-selection term. Position size doesn't change expected profit because the position is valued at fair value. Maximising each side separately gives a bid near 40 (noise-trader edge against informed sellers) and an ask near 61 (informed buyers only when settlement is above the ask).

Under that posterior, an ask below 80 mostly trades with informed buyers when the urn is rich in red, so it loses money. - **Ask:** Expected profit from selling at A is roughly 0.5·[Φ̄((A−F)/19)(A−F) + Σ_{10R>A} w_R(A−10R)/W]. Its derivative is close to zero around A ≈ 27.5, so an ask of 28 is near-optimal. Asks round up, so 28.
- **Bid:** Expected profit from buying at B is roughly 0.5·[Φ((B−F)/19)(F−B) + Σ_{10R<B} w_R(10R−B)/W]. For B ≤ 0 the informed term vanishes, and the optimum is near B ≈ −6. Bids round down, so −6.

{"bid": -6, "ask": 28}

Draw 1 was blue, so the posterior on red balls is proportional to (8 - n), giving a fair value of 10 × 7/3 ≈ 23.3. - **Ask:** an informed buyer only arrives when V > ask, which for an ask around 20 means R ≥ 3 (about 1% of the posterior). Noise buyers arrive with probability P(X > ask), and the expected gain (ask − 5.6) × P(X > ask) peaks near 20–21. Expected per-quote value is about +1.5.

I'm ending at ask 20 rather than 21 because the two are essentially equal in expected value. The short horizon (3 quotes after this one) and the draw-2 reveal before stage 3 are not modelled, so this is a one-shot optimum.

This is a single-quote, risk-neutral optimisation and ignores the two remaining quotes.
